item.title: Designing and Building My Own Ergonomic Keyboard – Part 1
item.dc:creator: lakshyajeet
item.description:
I built a 46-key ergonomic keyboard from the ground up, from designing the layout in Ergogen and modeling the enclosure in FreeCAD to 3D printing the parts and hand-wiring the switch matrix. It wasn't the cheapest keyboard I could have bought, but it is one that is quite literally mine.

The post Designing and Building My Own Ergonomic Keyboard – Part 1 appeared first on Lakshyajeet's Blog.
item.content:encoded:
I spend a fairly big part of my day sitting in front of a computer, and as a software engineer it usually means spending most of that time typing. At some point, I started paying more attention to the ergonomics of my setup, and perhaps a little more attention to my keyboard than I should have, not because the keyboards I own were bad, but more so because I wanted something to be mine. I wanted to design a keyboard around the way I work, the way my hands rest and the way I actually type. The angles, the split layout, the placement of the keys are all there for a reason; they make the keyboard feel more natural to use over a long period of time. And, honestly, building a keyboard from scratch sounded like a much more interesting problem than simply buying another one. It also turned out not to be the cheaper option, but that was never really the point. As a bonus, I got to learn more about the hardware side of things, something software engineers don’t often get a chance to interact with, and learn how to use CAD to design it.

Choosing the Hardware

Before designing anything or drawing the first line, there are a few decisions I needed to make. A keyboard is a relatively simple device when you think about it, but there are a few choices we need to make before we start. The switches determine how it feels, the microcontroller determines how it behaves and the physical construction determines how it all comes together.

1. Key Switches

There are many different types, brands, and feels available, but I’ll focus on four of the most common switch types here. There are multiple other brands and colors and feels available but these are a few of the standard one.

For my keyboard, I went with Brown switches. I wanted some tactile feedback while typing, as I don’t particularly like the feel of linear switches. That ruled out the Red and Black switches for me. I also find Black switches a little too heavy, especially when you’re typing on them for an entire day, the extra force adds up. I already own a keyboard with clicky Blue switches, but they are a little too loud for my preference, even when I’m wearing headphones. Since this keyboard was going to be used for programming for hours at a time, the balance between tactile feedback and noise made Browns feel like the right choice for me.

2. Microcontroller

The next decision was the brain of the keyboard. I already had a few microcontrollers lying around, so it was less about the “best” one to buy and more about figuring out which one made the most sense for my use case.

For this version, I chose STM32. The main reason wasn’t raw processing power, I wasn’t exactly building a keyboard that needed a powerful CPU. It was the ecosystem around it and how well it fit the firmware stack I wanted to use.

I also deliberately kept wireless as something I could revisit later. The ESP32 makes that tempting, and there are other platforms that are particularly well suited to low-power wireless keyboards, but for the first version I cared more about getting the hardware and ergonomics right than making it wireless on day one. Additionally, battery and BMS adds extra complexity which I didn’t wish to have right now.

3. How do you actually build the keyboard?

This is one of the most important decisions, and it is actually two different questions with overlapping answers. The first is about the body: how do I connect everything together? There are two main options:

Custom 3D printed enclosure

  • Completely custom
  • Easy to iterate on
  • Easy to make unusual ergonomic shapes
  • requires designing and printing everything yourself.

PCB based construction

  • Cleaner manufacturing
  • Potentially thinner/lighter
  • More repeatable
  • but requires designing the PCB and usually constrains the physical form more

Then the second question is, how do the switches connect?

Hand-wiring: Each switch is electrically wired to the controller.

Pros:

  • excellent for one-off/custom keyboards
  • no PCB design required
  • very flexible
  • easy to experiment

Cons:

  • lots of manual wiring
  • messier internally
  • harder to reproduce

Custom PCB: The switch sockets/components are mounted directly to a PCB.

Pros:

  • much cleaner
  • mechanically robust
  • easier assembly once designed
  • reproducible

Cons:

  • more design work up front
  • PCB manufacturing cost
  • changes to the layout become more expensive

Since this was a personal project and I expected to iterate on the design, I chose to 3D print the body and use a more DIY approach internally rather than immediately designing a custom PCB. That gave me the freedom to change the shape, spacing and mounting without having to redesign and manufacture a PCB every time I changed my mind,. It also wasn’t necessarily easier than designing a PCB; in some ways, getting the CAD right was even harder.

With those decisions out of the way, I finally had enough constraints to start designing the keyboard itself. I knew what switches I wanted, what controller I was going to use, and roughly how I wanted the physical construction to work. Now I could start with the part that mattered most: the layout.

Designing the Layout

I didn’t want to start with a conventional rectangular keyboard and simply split it in half. Since the whole point of building a custom keyboard was to make it more comfortable for me. The main typing area follows the way I naturally position my fingers rather than forming a perfect rectangle. That meant experimenting with the position of the keys, the angle of each column, and the placement of the thumb keys until the layout felt natural.

For this, I used Ergogen. It gave me a way to describe the keyboard layout parametrically rather than manually placing every key in CAD. I could define the columns, rows, spacing, rotations, and other geometric relationships, and then generate the resulting layout.

One of the first decisions I made was the number of keys. The final design has 46 keys, which was enough for the keys I use regularly while still allowing me to keep the keyboard compact. The goal wasn’t to reproduce every key found on a standard keyboard; instead, I wanted the physical layout to contain the keys I actually need and let the firmware handle the rest through layers and custom mappings.

The interesting part of using Ergogen was that I could treat the keyboard almost like a coordinate system for my hands.

Instead of thinking:

Where should this key go on a standard keyboard?

I could think:

Where does my finger naturally want to move?

That allowed me to experiment with different column angles and key positions. The main typing area follows the natural shape of the fingers rather than forming a perfect rectangle, while the thumb keys are positioned separately so that they can be reached without forcing the hand to move away from its normal resting position.

This was also where I started treating the layout as the foundation for everything that came after. Once the positions of the keys were fixed, those positions would determine the plate, the switch placement, the enclosure, and eventually the physical dimensions of the entire keyboard.

From Ergogen to CAD

Once I was satisfied with the layout, I generated the plate geometry and the switch positions from Ergogen and moved into FreeCAD.

At this point, the keyboard stopped being just a collection of coordinates and started becoming a physical object. I could now work with actual dimensions and begin figuring out how the switches, plates, keycaps, screws, and enclosure would fit together. The important thing here is that I didn’t design the enclosure first and then try to squeeze the keyboard into it. I started with the thing that mattered most, the key layout, and built the physical design around it.

That decision ended up influencing almost every part of the final keyboard.

After that, it became an iterative grind spanning a few weeks as I worked through the rest of the design before finally committing to a print. I started with the base plate, where all the switches would sit.

Using the base plate as a reference, I then designed the body around it.

Assembly

This is the fun part, once all the parts were designed and printed it was time to turn them into an actual keyboard. Since this was a one-off build, I decided to hand-wire the keyboard matrix.

The basic idea behind a keyboard matrix is fairly simple. Instead of running two wires from every switch directly to the microcontroller, the switches are arranged into rows and columns. Each switch connects one row to one column, allowing the microcontroller to identify which key was pressed while using far fewer GPIO pins.

For this build, I first installed all of the switches into the printed plate and then wired the switches together to form the matrix. The rows and columns were routed separately, with a diode added to each switch as part of the matrix circuit.

Wiring the Matrix

The wiring was probably the most tedious part of the build. With 46 keys, there are a lot of individual connections to make, and keeping track of them becomes increasingly difficult once wires start crossing each other.

I used 1N4148 diodes, with one diode associated with each switch. The diode orientation is important because it determines the direction in which current is allowed to flow through the matrix. Getting this wrong can result in keys being detected incorrectly or the matrix producing ghosting.

Connecting the Microcontroller

Once the matrix was complete, the remaining wires were connected to the STM32 microcontroller. The row and column lines each go to their respective GPIO pins, and the firmware uses those pins to scan the matrix and determine which key is being pressed.

At this stage, I didn’t immediately close the keyboard up. Before putting everything inside the case, I tested the matrix and checked the individual connections. With hand-wiring, debugging a problem is much easier when everything is still accessible than when the entire assembly is already screwed together.

I also checked the wiring for continuity and shorts with a multimeter before powering the controller.

Bringing It All Together

With the switches soldered, the matrix wired, and the controller connected, the keyboard finally started looking like an actual keyboard rather than a collection of printed parts and wires.

This was also the point where all the earlier design decisions had to come together. The plate had to hold the switches securely, the key caps needed enough clearance to move freely, and the enclosure needed enough space underneath to accommodate the wiring and controller.

Conclusion

And with that, the first part of the build was complete. What started as a rough idea for an ergonomic keyboard had turned into a physical, fully custom-built device. I designed the layout around my own hands, translated it into a set of CAD models, designed the enclosure around the actual switches and keycaps, 3D printed the parts, and finally hand-wired the whole thing into a working keyboard.

The final result is a 46-key ergonomic keyboard that is quite literally built around the way I work. There were plenty of small decisions, measurements, iterations, and a whole lot more soldering than I initially expected, but that’s also what made the project interesting. Every part of the keyboard, from the angle of the keys to the shape of the case, is something I could change because I was designing the entire thing myself.

But getting the hardware working was only half of the project.

A custom keyboard becomes much more interesting when you can also change what the keys actually do. In the next part, I’ll move from the physical build to the software side of the keyboard, including the microcontroller, QMK, custom keymaps, layers, and the firmware customizations I made to make the keyboard behave the way I wanted..

The post Designing and Building My Own Ergonomic Keyboard – Part 1 appeared first on Lakshyajeet's Blog.

item.title: Adding Interactivity on Static WordPress sites
item.dc:creator: lakshyajeet
item.description:
Learn how to add real-time search and comments to static WordPress sites using Supabase, Web Components, and automated bidirectional sync. Keep WordPress as your CMS while enjoying the speed, security, and zero-runtime-PHP benefits of a fully static site.

The post Adding Interactivity on Static WordPress sites appeared first on Lakshyajeet's Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Everyone knows the trade-off, static sites are the holy grail of performance – no database queries, no PHP processing, no server-side rendering. Just HTML, CSS, and JavaScript served directly from a CDN edge node. They load instantly, handle traffic spikes effortlessly, cost little to nothing to host, and have a near zero attack surface.
But the problem is: the web isn’t static. Users expect to interact with your content like searching content, leaving comments. These things requires a backend.
WordPress powers a huge portion of the web because it makes content management easy. The block editor is my favorite among the media library, user roles and taxonomy system. It is also incredibly mature. But WordPress needs a PHP runtime for processing each and every request, MySQL queries to be made within each request.
What if we could keep WordPress as our content management layer – write posts, organize media, use the block editor – but serve the site as static HTML? That is the question I set to answer with: WP Static Interactivity, a WordPress plugin that offloads dynamic features to Supabase, letting you freeze your WordPress site into static HTML while keeping it interactive.

Why Supabase?

Supabase is an open-source Firebase alternative built on PostgreSQL. Its features align perfectly with this use case:

  • Auto-generated REST API: Every table automatically gets full CRUD via PostgREST
  • Row Level Security (RLS): Per-row access control at the database level, so the anon key is safe to expose in the browser
  • Full-text search: PostgreSQL’s tsvector/tsquery with GIN indexes, built in
  • Generous free tier: 500 MB database, 5 GB bandwidth, enough for a personal blog
  • Edge-ready: Accessible from any HTTP client, including fetch() in the browser
  • Self-hostable: Fully open-source stack (Docker-compatible) that lets you run the exact same backend on your own infrastructure for strict data privacy, custom compliance, zero external telemetry, and no platform-imposed usage limits.

Supabase isn’t replacing WordPress. It’s a read-optimized, edge-friendly mirror that the static frontend queries directly from the browser.

The Split-Brain Problem

When you decouple WordPress from its runtime, you create a split-brain scenario. WordPress knows everything – posts, comments, search data – but static site knows nothing. It’s just HTML files on a CDN with no DB connection.

The challenge is: How do you bridge this gap without reintroducing the server costs and complexity which we are trying to eliminate?

Existing approaches have trade-offs:

  • Serverless functions: Cold starts, vendor lock-in, complex deployment
  • Third-party services (Algolia, Disqus): Expensive at scale, data lives on someone else’s servers
  • Page caching (Redis Object Cache): First visitor still triggers a full WordPress bootstrap; attack surface remains

None of these fully satisfy: zero PHP at runtime, self-hosted data, theme-compatible output, cloud-agnostic hosting, and a simple feature set.

The Solution: Islands of Interactivity

The plugin takes a specific architectural approach to the split-brain problem. Instead of trying to make WordPress run on the static site or replacing WordPress entirely, it introduces a third system that sits between WordPress and the static frontend.

What the Plugin Aims to Achieve

  1. Zero PHP at runtime – The static site should never need to hit a WordPress server. Every page load is pure HTML/CSS/JS from a CDN.
  2. WordPress stays the content management system – You still write posts, moderate comments, manage media, and organize taxonomies in the WordPress admin. No workflow changes for content authors.
  3. Supabase becomes the runtime data layer – Instead of querying WordPress’s MySQL database at runtime, the static frontend queries Supabase’s PostgreSQL database directly from the browser. Supabase is optimized for this: it’s always-on, edge-ready, and has built-in REST APIs.
  4. Theme compatibility without configuration – The site should look exactly like the theme intended. The plugin shouldn’t need to know anything about your theme’s HTML structure, CSS classes, or layout system.
  5. Bidirectional sync keeps everything consistent – Changes in WordPress (new posts, approved comments) flow to Supabase. Changes on the static site (new comment submissions) flow back to WordPress.

Why This Approach?

Why not a JavaScript framework (React, Vue)? The plugin uses vanilla Web Components (customElements.define(), <template>) for the reason: they don’t require any build step, no framework-specific rendering, light weight, and most importantly work on every page irrespective of how it is generated. Whether you export your WordPress site with Simply Static, WP2Static, or a custom build pipeline, the Web Components are simple JS and activate automatically when the page loads.

Why not a headless CMS (Contentful, Strapi)? Those replace WordPress entirely. The goal was to preserve the WordPress admin experience – the block editor, media library, and plugin ecosystem are too valuable to give up. WordPress remains the single place for content management; Supabase handles runtime data serving.

Why not Algolia for search? Algolia is excellent but expensive at scale (a personal blog with a few thousand searches per month would pay $50+/month). PostgreSQL’s built-in full-text search, combined with Supabase’s generous free tier (500 MB database, 5 GB bandwidth), is genuinely free for most sites. It handles stemming, ranking, weighted search, and GIN-indexed lookups without any additional service.

Why not Disqus for comments? Disqus injects ads, tracking, and third-party content. Your comments live on their servers, not yours. By storing comments in Supabase (your own PostgreSQL database), you maintain full data ownership and privacy.

Why bidirectional sync instead of a single source of truth? Because each system is optimized for different things. WordPress’s comment moderation interface (approve, spam, trash, reply) is mature and battle-tested. Supabase’s REST API is optimized for direct client queries. Rather than forcing one system to do everything, the plugin lets each do what it does best and keeps them synchronized.

Why not use WordPress’s REST API directly from the static site? That would require WordPress to be running and accessible, defeating the purpose of a static site. The whole point is to eliminate the WordPress runtime dependency.

The design philosophy is intentionally narrow. The plugin handles exactly two features: search and comments. It doesn’t try to be a full headless framework, a static site generator, or a page builder. This narrow scope makes it simple to configure, easy to debug, and reliable in production.

The Database Schema

In Supabase’s SQL Editor, we create two tables:

-- Search Index Table
CREATE TABLE public.search_index (
    post_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT,
    excerpt TEXT,
    featured_image_url TEXT,
    permalink TEXT,
    search_vector tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        setweight(to_tsvector('simple', coalesce(title, '')), 'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('simple', coalesce(excerpt, '')), 'B')
    ) STORED
);

CREATE INDEX search_index_search_vector_idx
    ON public.search_index USING GIN (search_vector);

ALTER TABLE public.search_index ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY "Allow public read-only access to search_index"
    ON public.search_index FOR SELECT USING (true);

-- Comments Table
CREATE TABLE public.comments (
    id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    post_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    author_name TEXT,
    author_email TEXT,
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE
        DEFAULT timezone('utc'::text, now()) NOT NULL,
    status TEXT DEFAULT 'pending'::text
);

ALTER TABLE public.comments ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY "Anyone can read approved comments"
    ON public.comments FOR SELECT TO anon USING (status = 'approved');
CREATE POLICY "Anyone can insert comments"
    ON public.comments FOR INSERT TO anon WITH CHECK (true);

The search_vector column uses GENERATED ALWAYS AS … STORED, which means PostgreSQL computes it automatically on insert/update. Title matches are weighted ‘A’ (higher relevance) and excerpt matches ‘B’ (lower relevance), set up for future ts_rank() usage.

The plugin operates in two key modes:

  • Server-side (WordPress admin): Uses the Supabase service_role key to push/pull data. This key is stored in wp_options and not exposed to the browser.
  • Client-side (static site): Uses the Supabase anon key embedded in edge scripts. RLS policies restrict what anonymous users can read and write.

Search: Syncing Content and Serving Results

When a post is saved, the plugin schedules an async cron event rather than syncing inline:

public function schedule_post_sync($post_id, $post) {
    if (defined('DOING_AUTOSAVE') && DOING_AUTOSAVE) { return; }
    if (wp_is_post_revision($post_id)) { return; }
    if (!in_array($post->post_type, self::SYNCED_POST_TYPES, true)) { return; }

    if (!wp_next_scheduled('dm_si_sync_post_to_supabase', array($post_id))) {
        wp_schedule_single_event(
            time(),
            'dm_si_sync_post_to_supabase',
            array($post_id)
        );
    }
}

Why async, I hear you ask? If Supabase is unreachable, the WordPress editor shouldn’t hang. The sync cron event runs after the HTTP response has been sent.

The cron handler builds a row with relative URLs for portability:

private static function build_search_index_row($post) {
    $permalink = get_permalink($post->ID);
    $parsed_url = wp_parse_url($permalink);
    $relative_permalink = $parsed_url['path'] ?? '/';

    $featured_image_url = get_the_post_thumbnail_url($post->ID, 'full');
    $relative_featured_image_url = null;
    if ($featured_image_url) {
        $parsed_featured = wp_parse_url($featured_image_url);
        $relative_featured_image_url = $parsed_featured['path'] ?? $featured_image_url;
    }

    return [
        'post_id'            => $post->ID,
        'title'              => $post->post_title,
        'excerpt'            => wp_strip_all_tags(/* ... */),
        'featured_image_url' => $relative_featured_image_url,
        'permalink'          => $relative_permalink,
    ];
}

Relative URLs matter. If your WordPress site uses a different domain in development than production (e.g., localhost vs example.com), absolute URLs would break. Storing the path only (/hello-world/, /wp-content/uploads/2026/01/photo.jpg) makes the index portable.

A page with the search slug (default: search) must exist in WordPress. Some themes don’t have a search.php template and rely on page.php or archive.php. Using a page ensures there’s always a fallback template. The template_include filter overrides which template actually renders. The plugin then forces the theme’s search.php template to load instead of the page template:

public function load_search_template($template) {
    if (!self::is_search_page()) { return $template; }
    global $wp_query;
    $wp_query->is_search = true;
    $wp_query->is_page = false;
    $wp_query->set('s', $_GET['s'] ?? '');
    return get_search_template();
}

Block Hijacking with Template Capture

This is the most important part, and it’s the secret sauce which makes the whole plugin work. When WordPress renders the search results page, the plugin intercepts the core/query block with inherit mode:

public function override_search_loop($block_content, $block) {
    if ('core/query' === $block['blockName']
        && (is_search() || self::is_search_page())
    ) {
        
        $template_post = self::get_dummy_post();
        $posts_with_thumb = get_posts([
            'post_type'      => self::SYNCED_POST_TYPES,
            'posts_per_page' => 1,
            'meta_key'       => '_thumbnail_id',
            'fields'         => 'ids',
        ]);
        if (!empty($posts_with_thumb)) {
            $real_post = get_post(reset($posts_with_thumb));
            if ($real_post) { $template_post = $real_post; }
        }

        // Render the block with just this one template post
        $GLOBALS['wp_query']->posts = [$template_post];
        $GLOBALS['wp_query']->post_count = 1;
        $GLOBALS['wp_query']->max_num_pages = 1;

        $query_block = new WP_Block($block);
        $template_html = $query_block->render();

        // Output the custom element
        echo '<dmsi-search>';
        echo '  <template>' . $template_html . '</template>';
        echo '  <div class="supabase-search-results">Searching...</div>';
        echo '</dmsi-search>';
    }
}

The fallback is get_dummy_post(), which creates a minimal WP_Post object with a placeholder title:

private static function get_dummy_post() {
    return new WP_Post((object) [
        'ID'           => 0,
        'post_title'   => __('Search Result', 'dm-static-interactivity'),
        'post_excerpt' => '',
        'post_content' => '',
        'post_type'    => 'post',
        'post_status'  => 'publish',
        'post_author'  => 0,
        'post_date'    => current_time('mysql'),
        'filter'       => 'raw',
    ]);
}

Client-Side Search Component

The <dmsi-search> custom element fetches results directly from Supabase:

class SearchIsland extends HTMLElement {
    async connectedCallback() {
        const query = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
            .get('s') || new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get('q');

        // Fill the search input for the user
        const searchInput = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('input[name="s"]');
        if (searchInput) { searchInput.value = query; }

        // Update the query title
        const queryTitle = document.querySelector('.wp-block-query-title');
        if (queryTitle) {
            queryTitle.textContent = sprintf(
                __('Search results for: "%s"', 'dm-static-interactivity'),
                query
            );
        }

        this.currentTerms = query
            .replace(/[^\p{L}\p{N}\s]/gu, '') // Keep unicode letters/numbers
            .trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);

        await this.fetchPage(0);
    }

    private async fetchPage(page: number) {
        // Build FTS query with prefix matching
        const ftsQuery = this.currentTerms.map(t => t + ':*').join(' & ');

        // Uses 'simple' config (no stemming) — must match the schema
        const endpoint = `${config.supabase_url}/rest/v1/search_index`
            + `?select=*`
            + `&search_vector=fts(simple).${encodeURIComponent(ftsQuery)}`;

        const response = await fetch(endpoint, {
            headers: {
                apikey: config.supabase_anon_key,
                Authorization: `Bearer ${config.supabase_anon_key}`,
                'Range-Unit': 'items',
                Range: `${start}-${end}`,
                Prefer: 'count=exact',
            },
        });

        // Parse Content-Range for total count
        const contentRange = response.headers.get('Content-Range');
        if (contentRange) {
            const match = contentRange.match(/\/(\d+)$/);
            if (match) { this.totalResults = parseInt(match[1], 10); }
        }

        const results = await response.json();
        await this.renderResults(results);
    }
}

The :* suffix on each search term enables prefix matching – searching for “deploy” matches “deploy”, “deployment”, “deploying”. Without it, to_tsquery() requires exact lexeme matches.

Range-Unit: items is a PostgREST extension of HTTP Range headers for clean pagination. Prefer: count=exact requests the total count in the Content-Range response header.

The search component then clones the captured theme HTML for each result hydrates it with the data from Supabase and display the results.

Comments: Bidirectional Sync

Comments are more complex than search because they require bidirectional sync between WordPress and Supabase. Two-way sync is required because comments can originate in two independent places, and neither WordPress nor Supabase can fully own the comment lifecycle alone.

Entry point 1: The static site (browser → Supabase)

A visitor loads a static HTML page from a CDN, writes a comment, and clicks Submit. That POST request goes directly from the browser to Supabase’s REST API. WordPress is never involved, there’s no PHP server to receive the request, no session to authenticate, no wp-comments-post.php to process it. The comment lands in Supabase with status = 'pending'. If there’s no pull sync, that comment sits in Supabase indefinitely, unmoderated, invisible to the admin, and never displayed (because only approved comments are shown).

public function push_comments_chunk($offset = 0) {
    $comments = get_comments([
        'post_type' => ['post', 'page'],
        'status'    => 'all',
        'number'    => 50,
        'offset'    => $offset,
    ]);

    foreach ($comments as $comment) {
        $supabase_id = get_comment_meta(
            $comment->comment_ID, 'supabase_comment_id', true
        );

        $entry = [
            'post_id'      => $comment->comment_post_ID,
            'author_name'  => $comment->comment_author,
            'author_email' => $comment->comment_author_email,
            'content'      => $comment->comment_content,
            'created_at'   => gmdate('Y-m-d\TH:i:s\Z', strtotime($comment->comment_date_gmt)),
            'status'       => $status_map[$comment->comment_approved] ?? 'pending',
        ];

        if ($supabase_id) {
            // Already synced — update
            $entry['id'] = (int) $supabase_id;
            Supabase_API::request('comments?id=eq.' . $supabase_id, 'PATCH', $entry);
        } else {
            // New — insert with WordPress comment ID
            $entry['id'] = (int) $comment->comment_ID;
            $batch[] = $entry;
        }
    }

    // Upsert batch with merge-duplicates
    $response = Supabase_API::request('comments', 'POST', $batch, [
        'Prefer' => 'resolution=merge-duplicates,return=representation',
    ]);
    // Store supabase_comment_id meta after insert
}

Entry point 2: The WordPress admin (server → browser)

An admin logs into wp-admin, navigates to Comments, and sees a list. They approve a submission, reply to one, trash another as spam. WordPress fires wp_set_comment_status, wp_insert_comment, or trashed_comment hooks. If there’s no push sync, those changes never reach Supabase, the static site would still show the spam comment and hide the newly approved one.

public function sync_comments_from_supabase($since = null) {
    $last_sync = $since ?: get_option('dm_si_last_comment_sync', '2000-01-01T00:00:00Z');
    $endpoint = 'comments?created_at=gt.' . rawurlencode($last_sync) . '&order=created_at.asc';
    $comments = Supabase_API::request($endpoint, 'GET');

    foreach ($comments as $comment) {
        // Check if already synced
        $existing = get_comments([
            'meta_key'   => 'supabase_comment_id',
            'meta_value' => $comment['id'],
            'count'      => true,
        ]);

        if ($existing > 0) { $skipped++; continue; }
        if ('trash' === $comment['status']) { $skipped++; continue; }

        $new_id = wp_insert_comment([
            'comment_post_ID'      => absint($comment['post_id']),
            'comment_author'       => sanitize_text_field($comment['author_name']),
            'comment_author_email' => sanitize_email($comment['author_email']),
            'comment_content'      => sanitize_textarea_field($comment['content']),
            'comment_date_gmt'     => gmdate('Y-m-d H:i:s', strtotime($comment['created_at'])),
            'comment_approved'     => ('approved' === $comment['status']) ? 1 : 0,
        ]);
        if ($new_id) {
            add_comment_meta($new_id, 'supabase_comment_id', $comment['id'], true);
            $synced++;
        }
    }

    update_option('dm_si_last_comment_sync', $latest_timestamp);
}

The Lifecycle That Requires Both

A typical comment’s full lifecycle crosses both systems:

  1. Create — Visitor submits on static site → lands in Supabase (pending)
  2. Pull — Daily cron or manual sync brings it into WordPress
  3. Moderate — Admin approves in WordPress dashboard
  4. Push — Approval status propagates back to Supabase
  5. Read — Next visitor loads the page, fetches from Supabase, sees the approved comment

Each step depends on a different system. Step 1 and 5 happen against Supabase. Step 2 and 4 bridge the gap. Step 3 happens in WordPress. Without steps 2 and 4, the lifecycle is broken — comments are created but never moderated, or moderated but never reflected.

The Same Problem in Reverse

Consider this scenario: an admin replies to a comment directly in the WordPress dashboard. The reply is a new WordPress comment that doesn’t exist in Supabase. If push-only sync is running, it sends this reply to Supabase. But what about the visitor’s original comment that was submitted on the static site? It’s still sitting in Supabase, unknown to WordPress. The push ran, but the visitor’s comment was never pulled in. So the admin can’t see the visitor’s comment to approve it, and the visitor never sees their comment appear.
This is why the manual sync is a two-phase operation: first push (send all WordPress comments to Supabase), then pull (fetch all new Supabase comments into WordPress). Both phases are required for consistency.

What About Search?

Search is mostly one-directional (WordPress → Supabase) because posts are only created in WordPress. The admin writes, edits, and publishes content exclusively through the WordPress interface. The search index only needs to follow – sync new posts, update changed ones, delete trashed ones.
However, even search has a subtle two-way requirement: if the Supabase table is ever reset or the schema is recreated, the data must be re-pushed from WordPress. The “Replace Search Index” button in the admin handles this – it deletes all Supabase rows, then re-syncs every published post. This is a manual, batch version of push sync.

Comments are fundamentally different because the creation point is split between the admin-controlled WordPress and the anonymous-accessible static frontend. That split makes bidirectional sync an architectural necessity, not a nice-to-have feature.

Security Architecture

Supabase provides a very good layered approach to security. Using key separation:

  • Anon Key (Public): Safe to expose in the static frontend code and browser fetch() calls. Its capabilities are strictly restricted by PostgreSQL Row Level Security (RLS) policies.
  • Service Role Key (Private): Kept strictly server-side within the WordPress admin environment. It completely bypasses RLS, granting full administrative privileges to sync content and manage the database.

Row Level Security (RLS) Policies

The database enforces fine-grained access control directly at the row level for all client-facing operations:

-- search_index: public read only
CREATE POLICY "Allow public read-only access"
    ON public.search_index FOR SELECT USING (true);

-- comments: public read for approved, public insert
CREATE POLICY "Anyone can read approved comments"
    ON public.comments FOR SELECT TO anon USING (status = 'approved');

CREATE POLICY "Anyone can insert comments"
    ON public.comments FOR INSERT TO anon WITH CHECK (true);

What the End Result Looks Like

With this plugin active, your WordPress site can be fully exported to static HTML. The static site:

  • Loads instantly from any CDN with zero server-side processing
  • Has working search powered by PostgreSQL full-text search
  • Has working comments that submit directly to Supabase from the browser
  • Uses the theme’s own HTML templates via the template cloning pattern
  • Stays in sync with WordPress for moderation and content management

The admin workflow is:

  1. Write and publish content in WordPress as usual
  2. Moderate comments in WordPress as usual
  3. Periodically re-export to static HTML or use a continuous deployment pipeline
  4. The search index syncs automatically on post save (async via cron)
  5. Comments sync daily via cron, or manually from the admin settings

Future Enhancements

Webhook-Based Sync

Instead of daily cron for pull sync, Supabase’s Database Webhooks could call a WordPress REST API endpoint immediately on comment insert:

register_rest_route('dm-si/v1', '/webhook/comment', [
    'methods'  => 'POST',
    'callback' => [$this, 'handle_comment_webhook'],
    'permission_callback' => [$this, 'verify_webhook_signature'],
]);

Challenge: WordPress must be publicly accessible for webhooks. For sites behind firewalls or local development, cron works universally.

AI-Powered Semantic Search

PostgreSQL’s pgvector extension enables embedding similarity search. Each post gets a vector embedding; queries get embedded at search time. Results come from cosine similarity instead of keyword matching.
Challenge: Embedding costs money (OpenAI/Anthropic APIs). FTS is free and surprisingly effective.

Dynamic Content Beyond Search and Comments

The same islands-of-interactivity pattern could extend to:

  • User login and auth via Supabase
  • Post reactions/likes
  • Newsletter signup (form → Supabase → WordPress)

The Takeaway

The split-brain problem exists whenever you decouple content management from content delivery. The solution isn’t a single source of truth – it’s a two-source architecture with a robust sync layer.

WordPress remains the authoritative source for content creation and moderation. Supabase becomes the authoritative source for runtime data access, optimized for edge delivery.

The key architectural decisions:

  1. Async sync – WordPress never waits for Supabase. Posts sync via cron; the editor isn’t blocked.
  2. Template cloning – The theme’s HTML is captured at render time, cloned client-side. Theme-agnostic without configuration.
  3. Key separation – Service role key never leaves the server. Anon key is safe because RLS enforces access.
  4. Standard web APIs – No frameworks, no SDKs. Vanilla fetch(), customElements.define(), <template>. Works anywhere.

The result: a WordPress site that performs like a static site, serves like a static site, and is secure like a static site — but has the interactive features (search and comments) that make a site useful.

item.title: Porting Gutenberg to Frappe
item.dc:creator: lakshyajeet
item.description:
Frappe’s default web page builder is reliable, but it often lacks the structural flexibility of modern block-based editors. In this technical deep dive, I explore how I ported WordPress’s Gutenberg editor into the Frappe ecosystem, reconciling React state management with MariaDB storage and bypassing the limitations of traditional WYSIWYG editors without sacrificing the robustness of the Frappe backend.

The post Porting Gutenberg to Frappe appeared first on Lakshyajeet's Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Building content-heavy web pages inside the Frappe Framework has relied on a familiar, battle-tested pipeline: a standard Web Page DocType, a Rich Text editor or serial page builder, and a Jinja template to render it to the end user. It works. It has powered thousands of ERPNext sites, documentation portals, and marketing pages. While it works, having used WordPress’s block editor, Frappe’s default editor feels too basic.

Like most of my projects, this one also started with a “What if…?”: what if we could have WordPress Block Editor’s editing experience inside Frappe?

I am well aware that Frappe Builder exists to solve exactly this problem. However, my motivation was two-fold: first, it was a fascinating technical challenge that gave me the experience to embed Gutenberg portably into almost any environment. Second, I wanted to achieve a specific balance, a lightweight, “editor-first” experience that remains feature-rich without the overhead of a full-scale site builder.

In this article, we will explore the mechanics of injecting a modern React-based editor into Frappe’s hybrid jQuery and Vue-driven UI, serializing block-delimited markup into MariaDB, and dynamically generating CSS via modern Vite asset pipelines.

Rethinking How We Build Content

For basic, text-heavy content like blog posts or standard “About Us” pages, the legacy WYSIWYG (What You See Is What You Get) approach works perfectly, It’s a familiar and low-friction way that doesn’t require complex state management or heavy client side JS to function.

However, as the requirements shift towards more complex pages like interactive landing pages, or documentation the limitation of traditional editor becomes difficult to work with and maintain.

  • The “Span Soup” Problem: Traditional editors lack structural awareness, when a user tried to build a complex layout with multiple interactive elements, they often end up fighting each other. This inevitably leads to “span soup”- deeply nested tags, forced styles and redundant content so that it does not break responsive design on mobile.
  • Performance and Editing Constraints: As pages grow more complex, it becomes difficult to manage and edit them, especially when we add more elements: complex layouts, interactive components, or nested containers, the editing experience becomes increasingly sluggish.

On a personal level, I just genuinely appreciate the Gutenberg component ecosystem, so why not use it? The WordPress block editor provides a beautiful, drag-and-drop authoring experience that content creators already know and love. I wanted that exact user experience, but backed by Frappe’s Python based backend.

Why WordPress Gutenberg in Frappe?

When looking to replace the legacy editor, the obvious alternative usually is to build a custom editor on our own, and as mentioned previously that is exactly what Frappe Builder has done.

So why did I choose to import @wordpress/block-editor into a non-WordPress, Python environment?

This is not a silver bullet, and bringing massive WordPress NPM packages into Frappe carries bundle-size overhead with it, but the architectural tradeoffs are actually quite favorable:

  • Zero-cost Abstractions (The Data Model): Gutenberg elegantly stores the block structures as standard HTML with annotated JSON comments (<!-- wp:paragraph {"align":"center"} --> <p>Text</p> <!-- /wp:paragraph -->). This means Frappe doesn’t need any complex relational schema or dedicated block table to store page data. It can store the entire AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) as a single Long Text string, and Gutenberg parses it back into a React state tree effortlessly.
  • The Component Ecosystem: By utilizing @wordpress/block-library, we instantly inherit dozens of highly tested, accessible, and responsive blocks (Code snippets, Tables, Columns, Audio, Video) without writing a single line of UI code ourselves. If someday we want to add our own block it is a very straightforward process as building a block in WordPress is quite easy and very highly documented.
  • Memory Safety & State Management: Gutenberg leverages highly optimized React data stores (@wordpress/data, built heavily on Redux principles), ensuring that even pages with thousands of nested blocks won’t crash the browser’s main thread. It handles focus management, history tracking (undo/redo), and deeply nested block state with incredible efficiency.

 Intercepting the Workflow: The Architecture

The main obstacle in integrating a React-based block editor into Frappe is the fundamental environment mismatch. WordPress Block Editor expects to talk to a PHP backend via the WP REST API. It expects WordPress global variables. Frappe, on the other hand, expects a Vue.js based frontend with a Python based backend.

So we basically want to “hijack” the standard Frappe DocType rendering cycle and inject a React root over the existing DOM.

To build this bridge, we intercept the standard “Web Page” DocType in Frappe using a client script (block_editor_web_page.js). Add a custom “Block Editor” option to the content type, create a custom DOM node, and mount our React application as an overlay to it and create few custom fields to store our content data in the backend.

// block_editor_frappe/public/js/block_editor_web_page.js

let editor_node = null;
let editor_manager = null;

frappe.ui.form.on("Web Page", {
    setup_editor: function (frm) {
        // We check if the Vite-compiled React bundle has successfully attached 
        // the mount function to the global window object. If not, the script fails gracefully
        // and falls back to standard Frappe rendering.
        if (!window.mountDMBlockEditor) {
            console.error("Block Editor React bundle is missing.");
            return;
        }

        // We utilize the Frappe form lifecycle to mount our React app.
        // We isolate the React DOM tree inside a dedicated 'editor_node' to prevent 
        // Frappe's global jQuery logic from accidentally mutating React's virtual DOM.
        if (!editor_manager) {
            editor_manager = window.mountDMBlockEditor(
                editor_node,
                {
                    // Pass Frappe's current DB state down into React as props.
                    // React treats Frappe's database as the single source of truth upon initialization.
                    title: frm.get_title() || "",
                    content: frm.doc.block_editor_html_internal || "",
                    route: frm.doc.route || "",
                    published: frm.doc.published || 0,
                    meta_title: frm.doc.meta_title || "",
                    meta_description: frm.doc.meta_description || "",
                },
                // The 'onChange' callback. Every time React's state changes (keystrokes), 
                // we push the serialized string back into Frappe's internal DocType state.
                // This ensures Frappe's native "Save" button still works perfectly if the user clicks it.
                (raw_content) => {
                    frm.set_value("block_editor_html_internal", raw_content);
                },
                // The 'onClose' callback hides the React overlay, returning the user to the Desk.
                () => {
                    editor_node.style.display = "none";
                },
                // The 'onSave' callback. When the user clicks the blue 'Save' button *inside* React, 
                // we push all final metadata up to the Frappe form and trigger a backend save.
                (title, rendered_content, route, published, meta_title, meta_description) => {
                    frm.set_value("title", title);
                    frm.set_value("block_editor_html_rendered", rendered_content);
                    frm.set_value("route", route);
                    frm.set_value("published", published);
                    frm.set_value("meta_title", meta_title);
                    frm.set_value("meta_description", meta_description);
                    frm.save();
                },
                frm.doc.name,
            );
        } else {
            // If the React app is already mounted in memory, we don't remount. 
            // We just trigger an update method to push new Frappe data down the tree.
            editor_manager.update(frm.doc.block_editor_html_internal || "", frm.doc.name);
        }
    }
});

The Legacy Stack Fallback: Notice how we manage the content_type toggle in the codebase. If the user switches the content_type dropdown back to “HTML” or “Markdown”, the script automatically unmounts the React node and restores Frappe’s standard editor options. This ensures backwards compatibility for older pages that were not built using blocks.

Deep Dive into Serialization

This is where the heavy lifting happens. Once React is mounted, the Gutenberg engine needs to parse Frappe’s raw database string back into a living React AST (Abstract Syntax Tree), allow the user to edit it in a visual canvas, and then serialize it back out.

To do this effectively and securely, we maintain two distinct, hidden fields in the Frappe Web Page database schema:

  1. block_editor_html_internal (Source of Truth): Contains the WordPress block grammar (HTML annotated with JSON comments). This is used strictly to re-hydrate the React editor. It is never shown to the public.
  2. block_editor_html_rendered (Production Output): Contains pure, sanitized, static HTML with all CSS utility classes applied. This is what the Frappe Jinja template serves to public visitors.
// block_editor_frontend/src/BlockEditor.tsx

import { parse, serialize, getSaveContent, type BlockInstance } from "@wordpress/blocks";
import { BlockEditorProvider, BlockList, WritingFlow } from "@wordpress/block-editor";
import { createElement, RawHTML, useState, useRef } from "@wordpress/element";

export function BlockEditor({ value, onChange, onSave }: BlockEditorProps) {
  
  // We lazily initialize the parser only once on component mount. 
  // 'value' is the raw string from Frappe's DB (e.g., <!-- wp:paragraph --><p>Hi</p><!-- /wp:paragraph -->). 
  // parse() tokenizes this massive string and converts it into a structured array of React BlockInstances.
  const [blocks, setBlocks] = useState<BlockInstance[]>(() => {
    initEditor();
    return parse(value) ||[];
  });

  // Every time the user types a letter or drags a block, this function fires.
  // We serialize the AST back to a WP-commented string and send it to the Frappe JS Bridge.
  const handleInput = (newBlocks: BlockInstance[]) => {
    setBlocks(newBlocks);
    
    // Serialization overhead is mitigated by React's batched state updates.
    const serializedContent = serialize(newBlocks);
    setIsDirty(serializedContent !== lastSavedRef.current);
    
    onChange?.(serializedContent);
  };

  // When the user hits 'Save', we must generate the final, clean HTML for the public website.
  // We recursively map over the AST. For each block, we map Gutenberg attributes
  // into actual frontend CSS classes.
  const getRenderedHTML = (blocks: BlockInstance[]): string => {
    const renderBlocks = (blocks: BlockInstance[]): string => {
      return blocks.map((block) => {
        // Extract attributes and inject dynamic layout classes (e.g., is-layout-flex)
        const attributes = {
          ...block.attributes,
          className: getBlockContextualClasses(block.name, block.attributes),
        };
        
        const innerHtmlString = block.innerBlocks.length > 0 ? renderBlocks(block.innerBlocks) : "";
        
        // `getSaveContent` executes the block's specific save() React function, 
        // stripping away WP comments and returning pure, production-ready HTML.
        return getSaveContent(
          block.name,
          attributes,
          createElement(RawHTML, { children: innerHtmlString }) as any
        );
      }).join("");
    };

    return renderBlocks(blocks);
  };

  // ... (UI Render Logic Omitted for Brevity)
}

Data enters as a raw string from Frappe, gets tokenized by @wordpress/blocks, is manipulated by the user inside the <BlockList /> canvas, and exits via our custom recursive getRenderedHTML function. This architectural pattern cleanly separates the editor’s internal state concerns from the public output, ensuring that the frontend website only ever renders clean HTML, requiring zero JavaScript on the client side to display the page.

The Build Pipeline / Orchestration

Combining a Python/Jinja backend with a modern React/TypeScript frontend requires careful orchestration. We cannot simply run a Node.js development server in production; the React application must be compiled into static assets that Frappe’s bench CLI can serve via Nginx or Werkzeug.

We achieve this via Vite, compiling the React application into distinct bundles placed directly into Frappe’s standard /public directory.

Furthermore, we solved a massive design problem during this build phase: How do we ensure the editor’s visual styles (colors, spacing, typography) perfectly match the public website’s styles without writing duplicate CSS?

In a standard WordPress environment, this is handled by theme.json. Because we don’t have WordPress, we created a single source of truth (editorSettings.ts) and built a highly custom Vite Virtual Module plugin to dynamically generate CSS at build time.

// block_editor_frontend/vite.config.ts

import { defineConfig, type Plugin } from "vite";
import { generateThemeCss } from "./src/utils/generateThemeCss";

// Vite plugins allow us to intercept imports at compile time. 
// We create a "virtual" module that doesn't actually exist on the hard drive. 
function virtualWpThemePlugin(): Plugin {
  const virtualModuleId = "virtual:wp-theme.css";
  const resolvedVirtualModuleId = "\0" + virtualModuleId;

  return {
    name: "vite-plugin-wp-theme-generator",
    resolveId(id) {
      // If the code requests our virtual CSS file, intercept the resolution.
      if (id === virtualModuleId) return resolvedVirtualModuleId;
    },
    load(id) {
      // When the React app imports "virtual:wp-theme.css", Vite triggers this load function.
      // We parse the JSON editorSettings and dynamically generate thousands of lines 
      // of CSS variables (--wp--preset--color) and utility classes (.has-black-color) in memory.
      if (id === resolvedVirtualModuleId) {
        return generateThemeCss();
      }
    },
  };
}

export default defineConfig(({ mode }) => {
  const isFrontend = process.env.BUILD_TARGET === "frontend";

  return {
    plugins:[
      virtualWpThemePlugin(), 
      react(),
      babel({ plugins: [["babel-plugin-react-compiler", { target: "18" }]] })
    ],
    build: {
      // We output the compiled React application directly into Frappe's app asset folder.
      // This allows Frappe's native web server to serve the JS/CSS without a separate Node instance.
      outDir: "../block_editor_frappe/public/vite",
      emptyOutDir: false,
      cssCodeSplit: false,
      rollupOptions: {
        input: isFrontend
          ? resolve(__dirname, "src/scripts/frontendStyles.ts")
          : resolve(__dirname, "src/main.tsx"),
        output: {
          // Predictable file naming ensures our Frappe Python backend 
          // can easily link these exact assets in the Jinja templates without needing complex manifest lookups.
          entryFileNames: isFrontend ? "js/block_editor_frontend.js" : "js/block_editor_main.js",
          assetFileNames: isFrontend ? "css/block_editor_frontend.css" : "css/block_editor_main.css",
        },
      },
    },
  };
});

To tie it all together natively, we leverage Frappe’s after_install hook in hooks.py to automatically trigger an npm install and npm run build via Python’s subprocess module.

Code quality is strictly enforced across the language chasm: ruff lints the Python logic, while eslint and prettier ensure the React codebase remains pristine, all bound together by a unified .pre-commit-config.yaml.

State Management: Passing Data Across the Stack

The “distributed state problem” is the bane of modern hybrid architectures. How do we get the DocType state from a MariaDB row, pass it through a Python controller, feed it into a legacy jQuery client script, and safely inject it into an isolated React context all while ensuring data remains strictly typed?

We solve this using a unidirectional data flow governed by a global window registry acting as an API boundary.

// block_editor_frontend/src/main.tsx

// We declare a global TypeScript interface. This creates a strict contract 
// so the legacy jQuery application (Frappe Desk) knows exactly what data shapes 
// it must provide to instantiate the React application.
declare global {
  interface Window {
    mountDMBlockEditor: (
      element: HTMLElement,
      props: {
        content: string;
        title: string;
        route: string;
        published: number;
        meta_title: string;
        meta_description: string;
      },
      onChange: (content: string) => void,
      onClose: () => void,
      onSave: (title: string, rendered: string, route: string, published: number, meta_title: string, meta_description: string) => void,
      docName: string,
    ) => void;
  }
}

let root: Root | null = null;

window.mountDMBlockEditor = (element, props, onChange, onClose, onSave, docName) => {
  if (!root) {
    root = createRoot(element); // Initialize the React 18 Root
  }

  // We destructure the database state passed from Frappe and inject it 
  // directly into the React BlockEditor as props. React now "owns" the UI state.
  const { content, title, route, published, meta_title, meta_description } = props;

  const render = (newContent: string, newDocName: string) => {
    root?.render(
      <StrictMode>
        <BlockEditor
          key={newDocName} // Changing the key forces a full React remount if the Frappe doc changes
          value={newContent}
          title={title}
          route={route}
          published={published}
          meta_title={meta_title}
          meta_description={meta_description}
          onChange={onChange}
          onClose={onClose}
          onSave={onSave}
        />
      </StrictMode>,
    );
  };

  render(content, docName);

  // We return an API object back to the Frappe JS script.
  // This allows Frappe to programmatically update the React state if the database 
  // changes via background events, or destroy the React instance entirely to free memory.
  return {
    update: render,
    unmount: () => {
      root?.unmount();
      root = null;
    },
  };
};

This unidirectional setup eliminates race conditions. React completely owns the UI state and memory lifecycle, but Frappe remains the single source of truth for the persistent data.

To serve this to the end user, we utilize Frappe’s Python override hooks. The backend implementation is intentionally minimal, acting only as a data router:

# block_editor_frappe/overrides/web_page.py

from frappe.website.doctype.web_page.web_page import WebPage

class BlockEditorWebPage(WebPage):
    def get_context(self, context):
        super().get_context(context)

        # If the user didn't select "Block Editor", we fall back to standard Frappe rendering.
        if self.content_type != "Block Editor":
            return

        # Inject the pure, rendered HTML into the Jinja context.
        # This completely bypasses the need for the frontend to run React to see the page.
        context.block_editor_content = self.block_editor_html_rendered or ""

        # Point the renderer to our custom Jinja template that includes our Vite CSS assets.
        context.template = "block_editor_frappe/templates/pages/web_page_block_editor.html"

The simplicity of this Python class is the entire point: the React frontend does all the heavy analytical lifting and serialization, and the backend simply serves the resulting static string at light speed.

Limitations and Future Enhancements

While I am extemely content with this implementation, but we must be honest about its current constraints. Mashing two massive ecosystems together results in inevitable friction points:

  1. WordPress API Reliance: Some native Gutenberg blocks (like dynamic Post Grids, Navigation Menus, or Search) attempt to fetch data dynamically via WordPress REST API endpoints (/wp-json/). Because Frappe doesn’t possess these specific endpoints, those complex dynamic blocks currently fail to render and must be filtered out of the block registry.
  2. Asset Management Disconnect: Currently, dragging and dropping an image into the editor embeds it as a Base64 string or relies on external URLs. It completely bypasses Frappe’s native File Manager DocType. This means images uploaded via the editor don’t show up in the standard Frappe file list, breaking centralized asset management and potentially inflating the database size.
  3. Environment Bypasses: If a user edits the block_editor_html_internal string directly via a Python script or the Frappe REST API (bypassing the React UI), the block_editor_html_rendered field will not update automatically, causing a synchronization mismatch between the database and the public website.

Where do we go from here?

  • Frappe Native Block API Middleware: We can build a custom Python/JS middleware layer that intercepts Gutenberg’s outgoing WP REST API calls and maps them to Frappe DocType queries. This would allow a native block to dynamically fetch ERPNext data (e.g., embedding a live, filtered grid of Item DocTypes directly into a Web Page layout). Instead we can also simply create new blocks for our usecase which do not even depend on WordPress APIs and used Frappe’s API natively.
  • Media Upload Bridging: We can also add custom React hook that intercepts the block editor’s image drop event, reroutes the file to Frappe’s upload_file endpoint, and returns the generated Frappe File URL back to the image block, perfectly synchronizing the two systems. Maybe we can have a Media Library modal equivalent here.
  • Code-editor Mode: Like in WordPress, adding a code editor mode here will be or very helpful for debugging and checking the exact markup generated by the editor.

Conclusion

Porting the WordPress Gutenberg editor into the Frappe Framework was more than just a pursuit of a “prettier” UI; it was a deep dive into reconciling two fundamentally different architectural philosophies. By successfully embedding a React-based, state-driven editor into Frappe’s jQuery and Vue-driven ecosystem, this project proves that we don’t have to choose between the robustness of a Python backend and the world-class authoring experience of modern JavaScript libraries.

While challenges remain, specifically regarding the alignment of asset management and the “hijacking” of WordPress-specific API calls, the foundation is solid. This integration opens the door for a new class of Frappe-powered websites: those that demand the technical rigor of an ERP and the aesthetic flexibility of a modern CMS.

Ultimately, this project demonstrates that with the right orchestration of build tools and state management, we can bypass the limitations of a “basic” editor and provide content creators with a truly professional, block-first experience without leaving the Frappe ecosystem.
