item.title: Mastering Context with Code Mode AI Agents
item.dc:creator: lakshyajeet
item.description:
AI agents in software development have evolved from passive text generators to autonomous systems. Code Mode agents reduce token bloat and context rot by dynamically executing scripts, while orchestrator-subagent architectures, skill injection, and secure sandboxing ensure efficient, scalable, and safe AI workflows.

The post Mastering Context with Code Mode AI Agents appeared first on Lakshyajeet's Blog.
item.content:encoded:
The integrations for Large Language Models into software development life-cycle has undergone a significant change in a very less time. In the emergent stages, the Language Models functioned as passive text generators or sophisticated autocomplete, relying entirely on constant human prompting and oversight.
However, the engineering paradigm has shifted towards autonomous, agentic systems capable of self orchestrating complex software engineering workflows without continuous human intervention. Central to this architecture is the establishment of universal integration frameworks, most notably the Model Context Protocol.

The Model Context Protocol(MCP) is an open, standardized architecture that allows an LLM to interface securely with external data sources, enterprise APIs, and local environments. It works by formalizing the communication layer between the underlying model and the environments. It allows developers to build systems not limited by an LLM’s training data, but instead are actively connected to real-time applications.

Historically, agents have interacted with these environments through a mechanism known as direct tool calling. Under this, developers are required to explicitly define a strict, deterministic JSON schema for every available tool, function or data source. The LLM would process the user’s request, generate a highly structured JSON response matching one of these pre-defined schemas, and the host application would intercept this JSON object to execute the corresponding function. While this deterministic approach proved to be highly effective for various applications, it tends to be the bottleneck when scaled to high complexity and high volume workflows.

Exposing a massive API surface requires injecting hundreds of lines of tool definitions into the model context directly into the model’s system prompt even if we don’t need to use most of the tools at any time. This approach leads to excessive token usage, higher processing latency and the worst of all, “context rot,” where the model’s self-attention mechanism degrades under the weight of excessive information, causing it to hallucinate and forget early instructions or leading to enter infinite loops.

To resolve these architectural bottlenecks, a new paradigm has emerged, referred as “Code Mode.” Rather than forcing the agent to select from a static list of pre-defined JSON schemas, the Code Mode paradigm provides the agent an interactive interpreter defined entirely by executable programming languages. Under this, the agent dynamically writes, evaluates, and executes scripts to discover tools, manipulate data, and interact with the external tools.

The architectural principles discussed here are heavily exemplified by my project repository at DarkMatter-999/Kymic,

The Latent Crisis of Context Rot and Token Inefficiency

To fully understand the need of Code Mode agents, we my identify the primary architectural problem with the current tool-calling mechanism. In the standard implementations, the client application is burdened with the responsibility of injecting every single tool’s description, parameters, data types and return structures into context using the initial system prompt. The model must retain all this in its active memory in order to successfully complete a task.

For complex integrations, like the complete Github API or Cloudflare API, this static injection technique consumes an astronomical volume of tokens. A large scale API integration can consume tokens equal to the total context size of the model, this problem gets amplified when there are more than one large scale MCP server installed, often consuming more that the total context limit of the model even before the user can enter their first prompt. This leads to the standard tool calling approach fundamentally unscalable.

Furthermore, traditional tool calling mandates that every piece of retrieved data must flow directly back through the model’s context window. In a standard workflow, if an agent queries a database to analyze performance metrics and receives an unformatted payload containing ten thousand rows of data, those ten thousand rows are appended directly to the conversation history. The model is then forced to read through this massive influx of noise to extract the relevant signals. This floods the context window, drastically increasing application programming interface processing costs, introducing severe latency, and drastically increasing the likelihood of context rot. Context rot occurs when the sheer volume of tokens dilutes the model’s attention mechanism; the model becomes disoriented by the vast amounts of intermediate data and forgets the user’s original overarching objective.

Context Efficiency and the Architecture of Code Mode Agents

The Code Mode paradigm, as implemented in this project, tries use to use best of both worlds, by altering the interaction dynamic but shifting integration burden away from static prompt to a dynamic execution environment. The fundamental concept is the the MCP servers do not add their extension array to tools to the models context at every request, instead the agent is provided with a minimial set of foundational capabilities. It is granted access to a JS interactive REPL environment, when the agent is tasked to solve a complex problem, it does not reply on pre-loaded knowledge of every system and tool. Instead, it writes a short, targeted script to query the available tools and capabilities and only use the required modules.

This on-demand discovery mechanism ensures that the models fixed token footprint remains virtually unchanged regardless of whether there are ten or ten thousand functional endpoints residing behind the Model Context Protocol gateway, despite of whether there are ten or ten thousand functional endpoints residing behind the Model Context Protocol gateway.

Empirical figures published by industry leaders demonstrate the absolute superiority of this approach. Implementing Code Mode has shown to reduce the token usage from 150,000 tokens to just under 2,000 tokens for specific data-heavy tasks, representing a cost-efficiency of over 98.7 percent.

Beyond raw token economics, the methodology fundamentally reduces the number of round-trips over the network required to perform multiple a complex chain of logic. By batching multiple operations into a single script, the agent bypasses the repetative tool selection loop. It can also execute conditional statements, parse intermediate results and reformat data as needed in a single step.

Exploiting AI Bias: Programming Languages as Native Action Spaces

Within the artificial intelligence safely and natural language processing, the concept of “bias” is overwhelmingly used through the ethical lens. Researchers extensively analyse and study how a model might inherit harmful societal stereotypes, unfair preferences or generate unequal representation based on flawed training data. However, for our purposes of agentic software engineering, there exists a secondary form of bias, which prove advantageous to us: the extreme statistical proneness of Large Language Models towards the formal programming languages.

Modern frontier models have been pre-trained on staggering amount of high-quality production code repositories. They have ingested terabytes of data from millions or repository covering virtually every major programming paradigm, library, framework, etc. Because the language model has seen so much code throughout its foundational training phase, its internal neural representations are highly optimized for structural logic, syntax, dependency management, and algorithmic flow.

This inherit AI bias towards code makes it perfect choice to define the entire agentic workflow. Because the model understands the execution environment it possesses the emergent ability to read, write, debug and self-correct code autonomously. In traditional architecture, if a JSON tool call fails the model struggles to work out why, leading to frequent possibly infinite retry loops. However, if a code execution fails it returns a standard stack trace pinpointing the exact problem to the model, it dynamically revises its script and continues with the execution without human intervention.

Orchestrator-Subagent Architectures and the Subagents MCP

While Code Mode drastically improves efficiency for individual agents, in reality for highly sophisticated tasks eventually exceeding the reasoning capacity of any single, monolithic model it bound to happen. When a single agent is tasked with simultaneously architecting front-end, backend, database migrations, security and test coverage, it is forced to balance the contradictory information leading to degraded performance.

To counter these limitations, the projects implements a Orchestrator-Subagent architecture. In this paradigm, a primary “Orchestrator” agent is deployed not to execute the granular tasks directly, but to function as an autonomous system manager and planner. Through this MCP server, the main agent can choose to spawn any number of sub-agents, delegating specific tasks to them. This provides advantages such as: Context Isolation and Parallel execution capabilities.

Every agent executes within its own completely independent sandbox. For example, if the main orchestrator agent identifies a security issue it assigns it to a subagent. This subagent is provisioned for this specific purpose and explores its domain without its context window being polluted by any other agent executing a different task.

Crucially, once a subagent completes its assigned task, it does not return its entire conversational history, trial-and-error logs, or intermediate failures to the orchestrator. Instead, the subagent acts as a context compressor. It distills its comprehensive findings into a highly condensed, relevant summary, returning only the finalized response regarding what it actually accomplished. This mechanism ensures that the main orchestrator agent remains exceptionally lightweight, agile, and completely free from context rot.

Dynamic Expertise Injection via the Skill MCP

In sophisticated agents systems, a very important distinction must be drawn between the fundamental “Tools” and applied “Skills.” MCP servers traditionally only expose the external capabilities, but this does not mean that the agent understands the optimal methodology for applying and using those tools. Instead of adding all the skills to the context, we again leverage the same idea as in the code mode. Through the Skill MCP, the model sees two primary tools: the ability to “search for skills” and the ability to “get info about a skill.” When an agent encounters a novel problem or is assigned a complex task, it initiates a workflow by first searching for skill using relevant keywords and then retrieving the exact skill it wants from the Top K results.

This perfectly mirrors the progressive disclosure technique, the LLM dynamically injects expert workflows into tits context window only when it is needed to solve a task at hand.

Transcending the Chat: The Canvas MCP and Browser-Native Interfaces

In a browser-native Code Mode implementation, the primary chat interface is strictly reserved for conversational dialogue, model reasoning, user instruction, and high-level progress reporting. However, when the agent generates complex structural output that cannot be easily comprehended as raw text, such as a dynamic data visualization, an intricate architectural diagram, an interactive code diff, a form, it utilizes the Canvas MCP.

The Canvas MCP operates as a stateful, interactive rendering engine. The agent emits structured html or writes front-end execution scripts that the Canvas MCP server instantly translates into visuals displayed in an interactive sidebar. This architectural separation of concerns creates a non-blocking user experience.

Defense in Depth: Node.js Virtual Machines and Docker Sandboxing

The immense utility of the Code Mode paradigm is directly linked to its greatest and most critical vulnerability: Arbitrary Code Execution. Because the entire architecture relies on the agent executing dynamic scripts to navigate its environment, discover tools, and implement solutions, any malicious instruction injected into the agent’s context could theoretically be executed by the underlying runtime environment.

Because the Code Mode architecture inherently involves running extensive file operations and explicitly grants the model the theoretical capability to change system files, a robust, defense-in-depth sandboxing strategy is absolutely mandatory. Operating system-level approaches that merely attempt to sandbox the agent process itself are fundamentally insufficient, as the agent continually requires active access to dependencies, networking interfaces, and file systems to complete its automated tasks. Therefore, the architecture employs a rigorous, multi-layered security model utilizing Node.js virtual machines, comprehensive Docker containerization, and strict directory confinement.

Tier 1: The Node.js Virtual Machine Isolate

For rapid, data transformation, mathematical calculation, string formatting, or purely logical operations, spinning up a full containerized environment for every single command introduces unacceptable, cascading latency. Instead, lightweight JavaScript execution is handled securely via the Node.js vm module, utilizing isolated V8 engine contexts. This allows the agent to execute raw code within a highly restricted, heavily monitored context that natively strips away all access to core Node.js modules, such as fs (file system access) and child_process (spawning external commands). Within this Node.js virtual machine isolate, the agent can parse complex JSON structures, manipulate data arrays, and verify algorithmic logic instantaneously, completely devoid of any risk of interacting with or compromising the host system.

Tier 2: Comprehensive Docker Containerization

While the V8 isolate handles pure logic, tasks that explicitly require CLI access, package installation, network requests, or complex multi-file compilation require a more capable environment. However, this environment cannot be the host machine. To counter the threat of system compromise, the entire application is run under a secure Docker container.

The agent is granted the autonomy to install dependencies, run test suites, and execute bash scripts, but it does so entirely within the bounds of the docker container. Even if an agent hallucinates a catastrophically destructive command, or falls victim to a prompt injection attack, the damage is strictly contained within the Docker container. The host machine’s kernel, personal files, and network credentials remain completely isolated and secure.

Conclusion

The transition from static, deterministic JSON tool schemas to dynamic Code Mode execution environments represents a fundamental maturation in the discipline of artificial intelligence engineering. By wrapping Model Context Protocol servers in executable programming paradigms, developers completely bypass the catastrophic context rot that plagues most advanced API integrations, achieving near-perfect token efficiency through progressive disclosure. This specific architecture succeeds precisely because it aligns with the inherent training biases of modern foundation models, which process programmatic structures natively and leverage standard execution traces for autonomous self-correction.

When this power is scaled, it inherently demands an orchestrator-subagent architecture. By delegating tasks through a dedicated Subagents MCP, the system maintains pristine context hygiene, compresses intelligence into actionable summaries, and leverages massive parallel processing to cut execution latency. Furthermore, by utilizing a Skill MCP, the orchestrator dynamically discovers and loads necessary workflows and enterprise guidelines only when required. The extension of this highly robust architecture to the web browser via dedicated Canvas MCP servers translates the raw, textual data into rich, interactive, and non-blocking visual experiences. Ultimately, the immense, unbridled power of arbitrary code execution necessitates uncompromising security boundaries. The meticulously engineered, hybrid approach utilizing Node.js isolates for synchronous logic, Docker containers for environmental virtualization, and rigid /tmp directory restrictions ensures that these agents can operate with unprecedented autonomy. This precise confluence of context efficiency, scalable subagent orchestration, dynamic skill acquisition, browser-native UI integration, and rigorous, multi-layered sandboxing firmly establishes Code Mode as the definitive blueprint for the next generation of secure, autonomous software development.

item.title: Rust in WordPress: The Architectural overview of CrabOptimize
item.dc:creator: lakshyajeet
item.description:
WordPress has relied on server-side PHP and C-libraries for image processing for over two decades. CrabOptimize changes the game by moving this heavy lifting entirely to the user's browser. Explore this technical deep-dive into how we bridge traditional PHP with a modern Rust and WebAssembly (WASM) frontend to deliver blazing-fast, multi-threaded AVIF and WebP optimization.

The post Rust in WordPress: The Architectural overview of CrabOptimize appeared first on Lakshyajeet's Blog.
item.content:encoded:
WordPress has run on PHP for over two decades. While the jump from PHP 7.4 to the 8.0x series introduced significant performance gains through Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation, the language still functions as a high-level manager for dynamic libraries built on C code (like GD and ImageMagick) to handle performance-critical tasks. CrabOptimize represents an architectural experiment: What if we offload this heavy lifting from the WordPress server to the user’s browser using Rust and WebAssembly (WASM)?

This blog explores the engineering behind CrabOptimize, a plugin that brings high-performance, fully client-side enhancements to the WordPress media library. By compiling Rust, known for its memory safety and speed, into WebAssembly, we bypass the limitations of server-side processing entirely. This not only reduces CPU requirements for the server but also modernizes the WordPress media workflow by introducing concurrent, multi-threaded processing on the client-side. This is a technical deep dive into how we bridge the gap between the traditional PHP backend and a modern Rust/WASM frontend.

Source Repository: DarkMatter-999/CrabOptimize

The Reality: Do We Really Need Client-Side Processing?

Let’s face it, the majority of WordPress websites aren’t being overwhelmed by hundreds of simultaneous image uploads. The majority of the time, only a few editors add media to an article. This has been handled flawlessly for years by WordPress’s built-in GD and ImageMagick integrations.

But sticking with server-side image processing comes with headaches:

  1. The Portability Nightmare: Portability is a pain. Server environments are all over the place. One host might run an ancient GD library. Another might have ImageMagick, but with missing modules for new formats like AVIF. Cheaper shared hosting can be even worse, with tight PHP memory limits that choke on large images.
  2. Bandwidth and Storage: New image formats like AVIF can offer a 10x to 50x improvement in file size compared to traditional JPEGs, yet many WordPress environments are stuck with rigid server configs, making it tough to switch to better formats. If you run a site with user-generated content or front-end uploads, this turns into a real problem.

But beyond solving practical problems, my motivation for this project was much simpler: I like Rust, and I like WordPress. Why not put them together?

Why Rust + WebAssembly?

If we want to process images before they touch the server, we have to do it in the browser. But why not simply use JavaScript?
JavaScript is undoubtedly quick. However, when you attempt to encode an AVIF image using complex matrix math across millions of pixels, native JS becomes slow. Additionally, it is by default single-threaded. We require a powerful tool that runs directly within the browser.

WebAssembly (WASM) provides near-native execution speed. However, it is not a language; rather, it is merely a compilation target. Other than the fact I like Rust, I chose Rust to build the engine as:

  1. Zero-Cost Abstractions & Speed: Without a garbage collector, Rust provides C-like performance. As a result, our compiled.wasm file is lightning fast and small (less than 500KB).
  2. Memory Safety: Processing images involves moving large amounts of raw data (ArrayBuffers) between the WASM module and the JavaScript heap. Rust’s stringent guidelines help us prevent memory leaks.
  3. The Ecosystem: The Rust ecosystem is fantastic. There are pure-Rust libraries (such as image and ravif) for features like AVIF encoding, and tools like wasm-pack and wasm-bindgen make life easier. There are also no messy dependencies on C code that are difficult to compile for WASM.

Intercepting the Media Library: Hijacking the Upload Stream!

It’s not easy to integrate Rust and WASM into WordPress’s media workflow. The primary obstacle? The sandbox for browsers. WASM cannot simply grab a file while it is uploading because it cannot directly interact with the DOM or network.

CrabOptimize uses a JavaScript “bridge” to address this. Before it ever reaches the server, it replaces the original image with the optimized one after intercepting the typical WordPress upload event and sending the raw file to the Rust/WASM module for processing.

Standard WordPress uploads flow directly from the User Interface (UI) to the PHP Server. UI -> FormData -> POST Request -> PHP ($_FILES)

CrabOptimize alters this pipeline by injecting a client-side processing step: UI -> Interceptor -> Rust/WASM (AVIF Conversion) -> Modified FormData -> POST Request -> PHP

We target two distinct upload mechanisms in WordPress: the modern REST API (apiFetch) used by the Block Editor (Gutenberg), and the legacy Plupload library used in the Classic Editor and Media Modal.

The Modern Stack: apiFetch Middleware

The Block Editor communicates with the WordPress backend via the REST API. Specifically, it uses the @wordpress/api-fetch package. This package supports middleware, allowing us to inspect and modify requests before they are sent.

In assets/src/js/editor.ts, we register a middleware that listens specifically for media uploads.

// assets/src/js/editor.ts

const mediaUploadMiddleware = async ( options: any, next: any ) => {
    // 1. Detect if this is a Media Upload POST request
    if (
        'POST' === options.method &&
        options.path?.includes( '/wp/v2/media' ) &&
        options.body instanceof FormData
    ) {
        const file = options.body.get( 'file' );
        
        // 2. Filter: Only process if it's a valid File object and optimization is enabled
        if ( file instanceof File && ! keepUnoptimizedFile() ) {
            
            // 3. The Bridge to Rust: processFile() wraps the WASM worker interaction
            const processed = await processFile( file ); 
            
            // 4. Client-Side Thumbnail Generation (calling Rust resizing logic)
            const originalDims = await getImageDimensions( file );
            const imageSizes = window?.dmCrabSettingsMain?.imageSizes || {};
            const thumbnails = await generateThumbnails( file, originalDims, imageSizes );

            // 5. Payload Swap: Replace original file with the WASM-generated AVIF
            options.body.set( 'file', processed, processed.name );
            
            // 6. Append Metadata: Send generated thumbnails as a JSON string
            if ( thumbnails.length > 0 ) {
                options.body.append( 'crab_thumbnails', JSON.stringify( thumbnails ) );
            }
            
            // Flag the upload so PHP knows to skip server-side processing
            if ( 'image/avif' === processed.type ) {
                options.body.append( 'is_crab_optimized', 'true' );
            }
        }
    }
    // Continue the request chain
    return next( options );
};

// Register the middleware
wp.apiFetch.use( mediaUploadMiddleware );

Key Takeaway: The await processFile(file) line is where the JavaScript thread yields control to the Web Worker running our Rust code. The browser UI remains responsive, but the upload request is effectively “paused” until the WASM module returns the processed binary.

The Legacy Stack: Hijacking plupload

The classic media uploader relies on plupload. Unlike apiFetch, plupload doesn’t have a modern middleware system. To inject our WASM processing here, we have to be more aggressive: we wrap the global plupload.Uploader constructor.

This ensures that any instance of a uploader created by WordPress (or other plugins) inherits our event listeners.

// assets/src/js/editor.ts

const hookLegacyPlupload = () => {
    if ( ! ( window as any ).plupload ) { return; }
    
    // Store reference to original constructor
    const OriginalUploader = ( window as any ).plupload.Uploader;

    // Overwrite with our wrapper
    ( window as any ).plupload.Uploader = function ( settings: any ) {
        const instance = new OriginalUploader( settings );
        
        // Inject our event handling logic
        setupUploaderEvents( instance ); 
        
        return instance;
    };
    
    // Maintain prototype chain for compatibility
    ( window as any ).plupload.Uploader.prototype = OriginalUploader.prototype;
    Object.assign( ( window as any ).plupload.Uploader, OriginalUploader );
};

In setupUploaderEvents, we bind to BeforeUpload. This is critical, plupload manages a queue, we must intercept the file object in the queue, pass it to our Rust worker, wait for the conversion, and then mutate the file object in the queue before plupload actually opens the network stream.

Server-Side Reassembly (PHP)

Once the Rust/WASM/JavaScript layer has done its job, it sends a POST request containing:

  1. The Main Image (now an optimized AVIF file).
  2. A JSON String containing base64-encoded thumbnails (also optimized AVIFs).
  3. A flag: is_crab_optimized.

The PHP side, class-media.php, acts as a receiver. It doesn’t need to invoke ImageMagick or GD. It simply saves the data it receives.

// include/classes/class-media.php

public function handle_thumbnails( $metadata, $attachment_id ) {
    // Check if client sent pre-computed thumbnails
    if ( ! isset( $_REQUEST['crab_thumbnails'] ) ) { return $metadata; }

    // Decode the JSON payload from the WASM client
    $thumbnails = json_decode( sanitize_text_field( wp_unslash( $_REQUEST['crab_thumbnails'] ) ), true );

    $file_path  = get_attached_file( $attachment_id );
    $upload_dir = dirname( $file_path );

    foreach ( $thumbnails as $thumb ) {
        // Decode base64 AVIF data back to binary
        $decoded_data = base64_decode( $thumb['data'] ); 
        
        // Write directly to disk - No server CPU processing required
        // ... (file writing logic) ...

        // Update WordPress metadata
        $metadata['sizes'][ $size_name ] = array(
            'file'      => $thumb_filename,
            'width'     => $width,
            'height'    => $height,
            'mime-type' => 'image/avif',
        );
    }
    return $metadata;
}

The Rust Core: Compiling Image Processing to WASM

We established how the upload process is intercepted by JavaScript. We currently have a File object in our memory. Converting that raw binary data (JPEG/PNG) into a highly compressed AVIF image within the browser is the difficult part.

Rust to WebAssembly (WASM) compilation provides speed that is nearly equal to native code. Additionally, you have control over memory and type safety, which JavaScript simply does not provide. The finest aspect? The user’s device, not your servers, is where all the hard work takes place.

The Rust Toolchain

CrabOptimize’s engine is a Rust library sitting in wasm/. We use wasm-pack to turn it into a .wasm binary and generate the JS “glue” code that hooks everything up.

In Cargo.toml, the crate-type is cdylib. That’s required for WASM modules that need to talk to JavaScript.

Here’s what makes this work:

  • wasm-bindgen: This is the bridge. It lets Rust and JS share complex data, strings, arrays, objects, without headaches.
  • image: A Rust library that decodes JPEG and PNG files into raw RGBA pixels.
  • ravif: A pure Rust AVIF encoder. It’s fast, optimized for WASM, and doesn’t need any outside C libraries.

The Optimization Logic (lib.rs)

The best part of the Rust toolchain is that we can simply mark any public function with #[wasm_bindgen] macro. This annotation tells the compiler: “Make this function available to JavaScript.”

Here is the actual implementation from wasm/src/lib.rs:

use image::load_from_memory;
use ravif::*;
use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn convert_to_avif(data: &[u8], quality: f32, speed: u8) -> Result<Vec<u8>, JsValue> {
    // 1. Decode the Input
    // We take a slice of bytes (&[u8]) representing the raw file.
    // The 'image' crate decodes this into a dynamic image object.
    let img = load_from_memory(data)
        .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?
        .to_rgba8(); // We need raw RGBA pixels for the encoder

    // 2. Prepare for Encoding
    let width = img.width() as usize;
    let height = img.height() as usize;
    let pixels = img.into_raw();

    // 3. Encode to AVIF
    // 'ravif' takes the raw RGBA buffer and compresses it.
    let res = Encoder::new()
        .with_quality(quality) // 0.0 - 100.0
        .with_speed(speed)     // 0 - 10 (10 is fastest/lowest compression)
        .encode_rgba(Img::new(&pixels, width, height))
        .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&format!("AVIF Error: {:?}", e)))?;

    // 4. Return the Result
    // We return a Vec<u8> (byte vector). wasm-bindgen automatically
    // converts this into a JavaScript Uint8Array.
    Ok(res.avif_file)
}

One of the most expensive operations in WASM is crossing the boundary between JavaScript and Rust, particularly when transferring big data sets like images.

  • Input: The file is read by JS into an ArrayBuffer, which wasm-bindgen allows Rust to view as &[u8].
  • Processing: The image is decoded into raw RGBA pixels by Rust.
  • Output: ravif compresses it into a new Vec<u8>, AVIF image.
  • Return: After Rust returns Vec<u8> back, and wasm-bindgen converts it to a Uint8Array for JavaScript.

This copy overhead is negligible compared to the time saved by using WASM for the compression algorithm itself when compared to JavaScript.

Dynamic Resizing in Rust

CrabOptimize doesn’t just convert; it resizes too. That’s handy for thumbnails and previews (more on that later). Here’s the second function:

use image::imageops::FilterType;

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn convert_to_avif_resize(
    data: &[u8], 
    quality: f32, 
    speed: u8, 
    target_width: u32, 
    target_height: u32, 
    crop: bool
) -> Result<Vec<u8>, JsValue> {
    
    let mut img = load_from_memory(data)
        .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;

    // Perform Resizing / Cropping using Rust's 'image' crate
    if crop {
        img = img.resize_to_fill(target_width, target_height, FilterType::Lanczos3);
    } else {
        img = img.resize(target_width, target_height, FilterType::Lanczos3);
    }

    let rgba = img.to_rgba8();
    
    // ... encoding logic (same as above) ...
}

The Hybrid Build Pipeline: Cargo meets npm

CrabOptimize’s development was not like other plugin projects. It is a combination of PHP, React, and Rust. Each feature requires working with code written in three distinct languages:

  • PHP for the server-side logic and hooks
  • TypeScript for the client UI and interception
  • Rust for the primary image processing system

It’ll be very repetitive and tiring if you attempted to manually construct every component-cargo build, tsc, copy files, and lint PHP. I therefore combined everything into a single build pipeline. All three languages are synchronized with a single command.

1. npm: The Brains of the Operation

We treat package.json as the main control. Although Rust has its own build tools, setup is made simple by using npm scripts to wrap everything. You’re ready if you have Rust and Node.js. The standard suspects, Webpack, Babel, and SCSS, are handled by @wordpress/scripts. However, it is unaware of our WebAssembly requirements. Thus, we include a pre-build phase.

// package.json

"scripts": {
    // 1. The Rust Step: Compile WASM first
    "build:wasm": "wasm-pack build wasm --target web --out-dir ../assets/wasm",
    
    // 2. The JS Step: Bundle TS and link the WASM glue code
    "build:js": "wp-scripts build --webpack-src-dir=assets/src --output-path=assets/build",
    
    // 3. The Combined Command
    "build": "npm run build:wasm && npm run build:js",
    
    // 4. Dev Mode: Watch for changes
    "start": "npm run build:wasm && wp-scripts start --webpack-src-dir=assets/src --output-path=assets/build"
},


The workflow goes like this:

  • npm run build:wasm kicks off wasm-pack, which compiles our Rust code (wasm/src/lib.rs) into a .wasm file and spits out the matching JS glue code.
  • npm run build:js fires up Webpack to bundle the TypeScript, which imports that WASM glue from the first step.
  • Webpack bundles everything into editor.js, ready for the browser.

2. Rust and Webpack: Making WASM Play Nice

Webpack doesn’t really know what to do with .wasm files, right out of the box or the glue code that wasm-pack produces. Things become jumbled even with Webpack 5’s experimental WASM support. With --target web, we allow wasm-pack to do the heavy lifting and provide us with ES modules that we can import straight away.
We load the module in our TypeScript using dynamic imports:

// assets/src/js/crab-worker.ts

// We import the init function and specific methods from the pkg folder 
// generated by step 1 of the build process.
import init, { convert_to_avif } from '../../../wasm/pkg/craboptimize_wasm';

// ...
await init(); // Boot the WASM module
// ...

This works because npm run build:wasm runs before Webpack starts looking for files.

3. Enforcing Quality Across 3 Languages

If you mess up in Rust, you can crash the worker. Screw up TypeScript, break the UI. Botch PHP, and you might take down the server. So, its good to be strict about code quality everywhere.

  • PHP: We use PHP_CodeSniffer and stick to WordPress Coding Standards.
  • JavaScript/TypeScript: ESLint and Prettier (through @wordpress/scripts) keep our React and TS code clean.
  • Rust: cargo fmt auto-formats our code, and cargo clippy catches mistakes and performance issues.

Multithreading in the Browser: Workers & Queues

We looked at how CrabOptimize generates a whole batch of thumbnails for every upload. When a user uploads a large raw image (20 MB), the browser must first decode it, resize and encode it multiple times.

The WordPress editor would simply lock up if we attempted to accomplish all of that on the Main Thread, which is the one running your user interface. No typing, no scrolling, and most definitely no “Publish”; a “Page Unresponsive” alert may even appear. Not the best. What is the answer, then? Web Workers are used by CrabOptimize to enable multi-threading. We approach the browser as a multilane highway rather than a one-way street. We distribute the workload evenly among CPU cores while maintaining a fluid user interface throughout.

The Worker: An Isolated Rust Environment

A Web Worker has its own memory and operates in a separate thread. It can run WebAssembly but is unable to access the DOM. Our Rust code is hosted by a worker script that we created in assets/src/js/crab-worker.ts.

  • When a message arrives, the worker unpacks the data: file buffer, file name, quality, speed, width, height, crop settings.
  • It loads the WASM binary only once per worker. No need to download it multiple times.
  • It converts the file buffer into a format Rust can process.
  • Then it runs the Rust code. This blocks the worker thread, but the Main Thread stays free-so the UI doesn’t stutter.
  • When it’s finished, it uses Transferable Objects to send the AVIF buffer back to the main thread. No copying, just instant memory transfer.
  • If something fails, the worker catches the error and sends it back. 
// assets/src/js/crab-worker.ts
import init, { convert_to_avif, convert_to_avif_resize } from '../../../wasm/pkg/craboptimize_wasm';

let wasmReady = false;

self.onmessage = async ( e: MessageEvent ) => {
    // 1. Unpack Payload
    const { fileBuffer, fileName, quality, speed, width, height, crop } = e.data;

    // 2. Initialize WASM (Lazy Loading)
    // We only load the .wasm binary once per worker to save bandwidth/time
    if ( ! wasmReady ) {
        await init();
        wasmReady = true;
    }

    try {
        // 3. Zero-Copy Transfer
        // We cast the buffer to a view that Rust can understand
        const input = new Uint8Array( fileBuffer );
        
        // 4. Execute Rust Logic
        // This blocks the Worker thread, but NOT the Main thread
        const avif = width > 0 && height > 0
            ? convert_to_avif_resize( input, quality, speed, width, height, crop )
            : convert_to_avif( input, quality, speed );

        // 5. Return Result
        // We use 'Transferable Objects' ([avif.buffer]) to move memory 
        // back to the main thread instantly without copying.
        self.postMessage(
            { 
                avifBuffer: avif.buffer, 
                fileName: fileName.replace( /\.[^/.]+$/, '' ) + '.avif' 
            },
            [ avif.buffer ] as any 
        );
    } catch ( err ) {
        self.postMessage( { error: err.message } );
    }
};

Performance note: That buffer transfer is crucial. By transferring memory ownership, we avoid the slow and wasteful process of cloning large images between threads.

The Queue: Managing Concurrency

We would undoubtedly run out of memory and most likely crash the browser if we started a new Worker for each thumbnail, perhaps 50 at once for a big upload. We use a scheduler (CrabQueue) for this reason.

Depending on the user’s hardware, CrabQueue regulates the number of workers that can operate simultaneously. In order to make efficient use of the CPU without overtaxing it, it restricts the number of concurrent tasks. Every time you add a task, CrabQueue decides whether to queue it or start it right away. It selects and initiates the next task when a slot becomes available. It looks for any pending tasks after a task is finished. Processing proceeds without overtaxing the system in this manner.

// assets/src/js/crab-queue.ts

// Determine logical cores. 
// Cap at 6 to prevent hogging all resources on high-end machines.
// Min at 2 to ensure some parallelism.
const MAX_CONCURRENCY = Math.min( navigator.hardwareConcurrency || 2, 6 );

export class CrabQueue {
    private running = 0;
    private queue: Array<{ task: () => Promise<any>, resolve: any, reject: any }> = [];

    // Add a task to the pile
    async add<T>( task: () => Promise<T> ): Promise<T> {
        return new Promise( ( resolve, reject ) => {
            this.queue.push( { task, resolve, reject } );
            this.process(); // Trigger the loop
        });
    }

    private async process() {
        // Stop if we hit the limit or run out of tasks
        if ( this.running >= MAX_CONCURRENCY || this.queue.length === 0 ) {
            return;
        }

        // Dequeue next job
        this.running++;
        const { task, resolve, reject } = this.queue.shift()!;

        try {
            const result = await task(); // Spawn the worker
            resolve( result );
        } catch ( err ) {
            reject( err );
        } finally {
            this.running--;
            this.process(); // Recursively check for next job
        }
    }
}

The Orchestration

When the user drops a file, processFile wraps the worker interaction inside a closure and submits it to the CrabQueue.

// assets/src/js/editor.ts

// Global queue instance
const crabQueue = new CrabQueue();

const processFile = ( file: File, ...args ): Promise<File> => {
    
    // We don't run immediately. We ask the queue.
    return crabQueue.add( async () => {
        return new Promise( ( resolve, reject ) => {
            
            // Spin up a worker for this specific job
            const worker = new Worker( 
                new URL( './crab-worker.ts', import.meta.url ) 
            );
            
            // ... handle messages ...
            
            // Send data to worker
            worker.postMessage( /* payload */, [ buffer ] );
        });
    });
};

The Result: Scalable Performance

By combining Web Workers with a Concurrency Queue, CrabOptimize achieves a balance between speed and stability:

  1. Responsiveness: The UI thread never handles image processing. The editor remains fluid.
  2. Scalability: A user on a powerful desktop (16 cores) will process images significantly faster than a user on a budget laptop (2 cores), as the queue automatically adjusts MAX_CONCURRENCY.
  3. Stability: The queue prevents “Out of Memory” crashes during bulk uploads.

State Management: Passing Data from PHP to WASM

We’ve got this lightning-fast image engine, but let’s face it: users don’t want a black box. They wish to change thumbnails, reduce file sizes, adjust quality, or maintain backups. All of a sudden, you’re dealing with a state management problem that affects the entire stack rather than just building an engine.

This creates a distributed state problem.

  1. The Source of Truth: The configuration lives in the WordPress Database (MySQL), managed by PHP.
  2. The Orchestrator: The upload logic lives in the Browser’s Main Thread, managed by JavaScript.
  3. The Executioner: The image processing lives in a background Worker Thread, managed by Rust/WASM.

Data must flow seamlessly through this chain: DB -> PHP -> HTML -> JS -> Worker -> WASM. 

1. The Source: WordPress Settings API (PHP)

Everything begins with the WordPress Settings API. Inside include/classes/class-settings.php, we register all the toggles and sliders users want:

// include/classes/class-settings.php

public function register_settings() {
    register_setting( 'dm_crab_optimize_settings_group', 'dm_crab_optimize_quality', array(
        'type' => 'number',
        'sanitize_callback' => array( $this, 'sanitize_quality' ), // Ensure 0-100
        'default' => 70
    ) );
    
    register_setting( 'dm_crab_optimize_settings_group', 'dm_crab_optimize_speed', array(
        'type' => 'integer', 
        'sanitize_callback' => array( $this, 'sanitize_speed' ), // Ensure 0-10
        'default' => 6 
    ) );
    
    // ... toggles for keeping originals, generating thumbs, etc.
}

2. The Bridge: Embedding State in the DOM

Browsers can’t directly reach into MySQL. So, we use send the settings by en-queuing the values inside scripts to pull PHP values and inject them as a JSON object on the window.

During the admin_enqueue_scripts hook, we fetch the values from the database and serialize them into a JSON object attached to the global window object.

// include/classes/class-assets.php

public function enqueue_settings_script() {
    // 1. Fetch from DB
    $quality = (float) get_option( 'dm_crab_optimize_quality', 70 );
    $speed   = (int) get_option( 'dm_crab_optimize_speed', 6 );
    $sizes   = wp_get_registered_image_subsizes();

    // 2. Serialize to JSON
    $data = array(
        'quality'            => $quality,
        'speed'              => $speed,
        'imageSizes'         => $sizes,
        'saveUnoptimized'    => (bool) get_option( 'dm_crab_optimize_keep_optimized', 0 ),
        'generateThumbnails' => (bool) get_option( 'dm_crab_optimize_generate_thumbnails', 0 ),
    );

    // 3. Inject into HTML head
    wp_add_inline_script(
        'dm-crab-settings-main',
        'window.dmCrabSettingsMain = ' . wp_json_encode( $data ) . ';',
        'before'
    );
}

The Orchestrator: Type-Safe Access (TypeScript)

In our TypeScript source, we define an interface for this global object to ensure type safety. We avoid accessing window.dmCrabSettingsMain directly throughout the codebase; instead, we use helper accessors.

// assets/src/js/settings.ts

interface CrabSettings {
    quality: number;
    speed: number;
    saveUnoptimized: boolean;
    // ...
}

declare global {
    interface Window {
        dmCrabSettingsMain: CrabSettings;
    }
}

export const getQualitySetting = (): number => {
    // Robust fallback if the localized script fails
    const q = window?.dmCrabSettingsMain?.quality;
    return ( typeof q === 'number' ) ? Math.max( 0, Math.min( 100, q ) ) : 70;
};

export const getSpeedSetting = (): number => {
    const s = window?.dmCrabSettingsMain?.speed;
    return ( typeof s === 'number' ) ? Math.max( 0, Math.min( 10, s ) ) : 6;
};

4. The Crossing: Main Thread to Worker

This is the critical bottleneck. Web Workers do not share the window object. The worker thread has no access to window.dmCrabSettingsMain.

If we tried to read getQualitySetting() inside crab-worker.ts, it would crash.

Therefore, the Main Thread must read the configuration and pass it as a message payload to the worker for every single job.

// assets/src/js/editor.ts (Main Thread)

const processFile = ( file: File ): Promise<File> => {
    return crabQueue.add( async () => {
        // ... worker setup ...
        
        worker.postMessage( {
            fileBuffer: buffer,

            quality: getQualitySetting(), // Reads from window
            speed: getSpeedSetting(),     // Reads from window
            // ...
        }, [ buffer ] );
    });
};

5. The Execution: Rust Consumption

Finally, the crab-worker.ts receives the message and invokes the Rust function. The Rust function signature in lib.rs was designed specifically to accept these dynamic parameters.

// wasm/src/lib.rs

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn convert_to_avif(
    data: &[u8], 
    quality: f32, // Received from JS -> Worker -> Rust
    speed: u8     // Received from JS -> Worker -> Rust
) -> Result<Vec<u8>, JsValue> {
    
    let res = Encoder::new()
        .with_quality(quality)
        .with_speed(speed)
        .encode_rgba(...)
    
    // ...
}

Limitations and Future Enhancements

CrabOptimize started as an experiment to bridge Rust, WebAssembly, and WordPress, but it has rapidly evolved into a comprehensive optimization suite. With recent updates, the plugin now supports bulk migration of existing media, allows choosing between AVIF and WebP, and respects filetype exclusions to skip optimization for specific formats.

However, shifting the heavy lifting from the server to the client-side is not a silver bullet. This architecture introduces its own unique set of challenges. Let’s look at the current limitations of this approach and where the project is headed next.

The Limitations of Client-Side Processing

1. The “Browser-Tab” Bottleneck for Bulk Migrations
While the newly added bulk migration tool is fantastic for retroactively optimizing your media library, it is entirely bound to the browser’s lifecycle. Because the processing happens via WASM and Web Workers on the client device, the user must keep the WordPress admin tab open. If the browser is closed or the device goes to sleep, the migration halts.

2. Invisible Uploads (WP-CLI and Server-Side Integrations)
CrabOptimize works its magic by hijacking browser events (apiFetch and plupload). But what happens if an image never touches the browser? If a plugin automatically pulls images from an external API, or if a developer imports media via WP-CLI, the browser is completely bypassed. These uploads will fallback to WordPress’s default server-side processing, missing out on our Rust/WASM optimizations.

3. Hardware Disparities and Mobile Browsers
While the CrabQueue dynamically limits concurrency based on the device’s CPU cores, compiling large images into AVIF or WebP is still a mathematically intense task. A user uploading a batch of 20MB raw images from an older mobile phone or a low-end laptop will experience significantly slower processing times compared to someone on an flagship machine. It costs the server nothing, but it taxes the user’s battery and CPU.

Future Enhancements: Where Do We Go From Here?

1. A Hybrid Fallback Engine (Server-Side Rust)
To catch uploads generated by WP-CLI, REST API integrations, or weak mobile devices, we could introduce a hybrid architecture. If CrabOptimize detects that the client-side environment is unsuitable, or bypassed entirely, it could fallback to a pre-compiled server-side Rust binary or a graceful PHP degradation to process the image natively on the server.

2. Dynamic WASM Module Loading
Now that the plugin supports both AVIF and WebP, our .wasm binary has grown because it must bundle the logic for multiple codecs. As we add support for future formats like JPEG XL (JXL), we risk bloating the initial plugin download. A future enhancement will involve Code Splitting for WebAssembly: dynamically fetching only the specific .wasm codec the user has selected in their settings, keeping the initial payload incredibly lightweight.

3. Advanced Client-Side Manipulation
Since we already have raw RGBA pixels loaded into memory inside a secure Rust environment, the possibilities for client-side image manipulation are endless. Future updates could include:

  • Privacy First: Stripping sensitive EXIF data (like GPS coordinates) before the image ever hits the network.
  • On-the-fly Watermarking: Applying text or image watermarks natively in the browser via Rust’s image crate.
  • Smart Cropping: Using lightweight algorithms to detect the focal point of an image and cropping thumbnails intelligently, all without touching the server’s CPU.

CrabOptimize proves that the browser is no longer just a client for WordPress, it’s a powerful edge-computing node. By combining the safety of Rust with the ubiquity of WebAssembly, we are just scratching the surface of what modern WordPress development can look like.

item.content:encoded:
Distributed Hash Tables (DHTs) are the backbone of decentralized file systems (like IPFS) and peer-to-peer networks (like BitTorrent). However, implementing one from scratch is often daunting due to the complexity of node discovery, routing, and NAT traversal.

The WebRTC-DHT project offers a clean, educational implementation of the Kademlia protocol running on Node.js. It leverages WebRTC for peer-to-peer data transport allowing for NAT traversal via STUN and introduces a hybrid signalling mechanism that transitions from a centralized WebSocket server to a fully decentralized mesh.

In this article, we will dissect the architecture, explore the core Kademlia logic, and understand how to orchestrate a P2P swarm using Docker.

All the code is available at the Github Repo: DarkMatter-999/WebRTC-DHT

The Problem, The Solution, and The Architecture

Distributed systems are notoriously difficult to build. If we want to create a database where data is shared across let’s say 100 computers, and any 10 of them disappear at any moment without losing data, we face three massive challenges.

  • Discovery: How do nodes find each other?
  • Connectivity: How do they talk to each other?
  • Routing: How do they find specific nodes with the data we want?

WebRTC-DHT is a reference implementation that solves these challenges using Kademlia (the routing algorithm behind BitTorrent) and WebRTC (for peer-to-peer connectivity).

What are we building?

We are looking at a Node.js based Distributed Hash Table (DHT).
Think of a standard JavaScript Map:

const map = new Map();
map.set('my-key', 'my-value');

This data lives in the memory of one computer. If that computer crashes, the data is gone.

In this project, we are building a network where that Map is sliced up and spread across hundreds of peers. So that when we run:

node.storeValue('my-key', 'my-value');

The system calculates the hash of 'my-key', finds the peers/nodes in the network whose IDs are mathematically “closest” to that hash, and stores the data on them.

The Tech Stack

The project relies on a few specific libraries to make this happen. To keep the implementation bare-bones and educational, the project relies on only a few essential libraries:

  • wrtc: This is a Node.js binding for the WebRTC API. Usually, WebRTC is for browsers (Chrome/Firefox), but this library lets our Node.js server processes act like browsers to establish Peer-to-Peer (P2P) data channels.
  • ws: A standard WebSocket library. We use this only for the initial handshake (signalling).
  • Docker: This is used to provide orchestration layer to simulate a whole network on our machine.

Architecture & File Structure

A. The “Physical” Layer (Networking)

  • The Signalling server is a centralized WebSocket server(src/signalling/index.js). Nodes connect here first to say “I exist.” It introduces them to their first few peers, then steps back.
  • The Connection Manager class(src/peer/connection-manager.js) handles the dirty work of WebRTC. It manages ICE candidates, SDP offers, and maintains the list of open sockets (DataChannels) to other peers.

B. The “Logical” Layer (Kademlia)

  • The Routing Table(src/peer/routing-table.js) it doesn’t send data, it just remembers who we know. It organizes peers into “Buckets” based on their ID distance. This is pure Kademlia logic.
  • The nodes speak a custom binary protocol to save bandwidth. The utility functions convert JavaScript objects into compact Buffers (e.g., packing a STORE command into bytes).

C. The “Application” Layer (The Brain)

  • The Peer Node class(src/peer/peer-node.js). This ties everything together. It owns the Storage (the actual data), runs the Routing Table, and executes the complex algorithms to find data (findValue) or store it (storeValue).

Now, with the basics all clear we can move to nuts and bolts of the system.

Networking & Hybrid Signalling

In a distributed network, the hardest part is often just saying “Hello.”

This project uses WebRTC, which is famous for its ability to punch through firewalls and offers a P2P connection between the nodes. But, this P2P connection starts with a catch, before any two peers can connect directly, they must exchange setup data (SDP offers, Answers and ICE candidates), this process is done through a third-party called Signalling.

While most implementation of WebRTC stick with a permanent WebSocket server in the middle for signalling, going with the spirit of decentralization and to avoid a single point of failure, we use a Hybrid Strategy.

  1. Bootstrap: Use a WebSocket server to find the first few peers.
  2. Decentralization: Once connected, use the existing peer connections to route signals and offers to new peers.

The Signalling Server

Open src/signalling/index.js, you might be surprised to see by how small the file is (~100 lines). That’s intentional as this server is dumb. It does not know anything about the DHT logic, it just passes notes between the peers.
When a node starts, it first connects here.

  1. Register: The node sends type: 'register' with its ID.
  2. Discovery: The node sends type: 'get-peers'.
  3. Introduction: The server calculates the XOR distance between the requester and everyone else it knows, returning the 5 closest peers.
// src/signalling/index.js (Excerpt)
case 'get-peers':
  // ... (logic to calculate distance) ...
  // Return top 5 closest peers so the new node has someone to talk to
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'peers', peers: closestPeers }));
  break;

Once the node receives this list, it disconnects from the logic of the server and moves to the ConnectionManager.

The Switchboard: ConnectionManager

The heavy lifting happens in src/peer/connection-manager.js. This class manages the lifecycle of peer connections.

The most critical function in this file is _sendSignal. This function decides how to send the connection setup data to a target peer.

// src/peer/connection-manager.js

_sendSignal(peerIdHex, type, payload) {
  // STRATEGY 1: The Easy Way
  // If we are still connected to the WebSocket server, use it.
  if (WebSocket.OPEN === this.socket?.readyState) {
    this._sendSignalWS(wstype, peerIdHex, payload);
    return;
  }

  // STRATEGY 2: The Decentralized Way (The Cool Part)
  // If no server, we route the signal through the DHT mesh we already have!
  if (!this.routeSignal) return; // (Safety check)

  // Wrap the signal in a DHT packet
  const msg = encodeSignal(type, {
    from: this.nodeIdHex,
    to: peerIdHex,
    payload,
  });

  // Ask the routing table: "Who is closest to this target peer?"
  const next = this.routeSignal(peerIdHex);

  // Send the signal to those neighbors, asking them to forward it.
  for (const hex of next) {
    const peer = this.peers.get(hex);
    if (peer?.channel?.readyState === 'open') {
      peer.channel.send(msg);
    }
  }
}

This is the key to decentralization. Once we have a few friends in the network, we no longer need the signalling server. If we want to connect to a stranger, we just ask our friends to pass the note along until it reaches the stranger, Kademlia makes it very efficient by organizing the network into a structured Distributed Hash Table (DHT) where every participant is assigned a unique ID. Instead of broadcasting a request to everyone or wandering aimlessly through a list of friends.

Kademlia uses a logical distance metric (XOR) to “map” the network, when you ask your friends to pass a note, they don’t just pass it to anyone, they pass it to the person they know whose ID is numerically “closer” to the stranger’s ID. This creates a routing system where the number of hops required to find anyone stays very small, specifically scaling at a rate of O(log n), meaning even in a network of millions, you can reach a stranger in just a few steps.

Handling Incoming Signals

When a signal arrives (either via WebSocket or forwarded by another peer), _handleDhtSignal processes it.
There is a subtle but important piece of code here for Deduplication. In a mesh network, you might receive the same forwarded message from three different neighbors. We must process it only once.

// src/peer/connection-manager.js

async _handleDhtSignal(buf) {
  const { type, payload } = decodeSignal(buf);
  const { messageId } = payload;

  // Have we seen this message ID recently?
  const now = Date.now();
  const ts = this.seenSignalIds.get(messageId);
  if (ts && now - ts < SEEN_SIGNAL_TTL) return; // Ignore duplicate

  this.seenSignalIds.set(messageId, now); // Mark as seen

  // Is this meant for me?
  if (payload.to !== this.nodeIdHex) {
    // Forwarding logic would go here
    // ...
    return;
  }

  // It is for me! Process the Offer/Answer/ICE...
}

The Routing Table

Now that our nodes can exchange binary messages, they need to know who to send those messages to. If we have 10,000 nodes in a network, we can’t simply keep a list of everyone in memory, that doesn’t scale.
Instead, Kademlia uses a clever strategy: Know a lot about your neighbors, and a little about everyone else.

This logic lives in src/peer/routing-table.js. It is arguably the most mathematically interesting part of the project.

The Metric: XOR Distance

How do we define “distance” on internet? Latency? Hops? Geographical location?
Kademlia ignores all of that. It defines the distance purely mathematically using the XOR operation on Node IDs.

If Node A is 0101 and Node B is 0100, the distance between them is 0001.

This has a powerful property of Unidirectionality. For any point x and distance d, there is exactly one point y such that distance(x, y) = d. This eliminates “routing loops” naturally.

In src/peer/utils.js, we see the raw buffer implementation:

// src/peer/utils.js

export function xorDistance(a, b) {
  const buf = Buffer.alloc(a.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    buf[i] = a[i] ^ b[i]; // Bitwise XOR
  }
  return buf;
}

K-Buckets

The routing table isn’t just one big list. It is an array of Buckets.
Since our Node IDs are 256 bits (SHA-256), the routing table has 256 buckets.

  • Bucket 0: Stores nodes that share the first 0 bits with us (very far away).
  • Bucket 255: Stores nodes that differ only at the very last bit (immediate neighbors).

This creates a logarithmic view of the network. We have highly detailed knowledge of nodes close to us, and sparse knowledge of nodes far away.

How do we decide which bucket a peer goes into? We find the First Differing Bit (or leading zero count of the XOR distance).

// src/peer/routing-table.js

_bucketIndex(nodeId) {
  const dist = xorDistance(this.nodeId, nodeId);

  // Scan byte by byte
  for (let i = 0; i < dist.length; i++) {
    if (dist[i] === 0) continue; // Bytes are identical, keep going

    // Found a differing byte, now find the specific bit
    for (let bit = 0; bit < 8; bit++) {
      if (dist[i] & (0x80 >> bit)) {
        return i * 8 + bit; // Return the exact bit position (0-255)
      }
    }
  }
  return this.buckets.length - 1;
}

Managing Buckets: The “k=20” Rule

Each bucket has a size limit, usually denoted as the k (default is 20 in this project).
Why limit it, you might ask? To keep the traffic low. If we know 20 nodes in a specific region of the ID space, that is statistically enough to route messages successfully even if half of them go offline any time.

But what happens when we meet a new node and the corresponding bucket is Full? This is where Kademlia’s “Eviction Policy” comes in.

The “Wait and See” Strategy

We do not simply drop the new node. Nor do we blindly drop the old node. We favor stability (old reliable nodes) over novelty (new unverified nodes).

  1. Update: If the node is already in the bucket, move it to the tail (mark as recently seen).
  2. Add: If the bucket has space (< 20), just add it.
  3. Standby: If the bucket is Full, we put the new node into a separate replacements list.
// src/peer/routing-table.js (Excerpt)

if (bucket.nodes.length < this.k) {
  bucket.nodes.push(nodeId);
  return { action: 'added' };
}

// Bucket is full. Don't add yet. Store as a replacement candidate.
if (!bucket.replacements.some((id) => id.equals(nodeId))) {
  bucket.replacements.push(nodeId);
  // Keep the replacement list small too
  if (bucket.replacements.length > this.k) {
    bucket.replacements.shift();
  }
}
return { action: 'full', bucketIndex: i };

So when does the new node actually get in?
Later, in the background, PeerNode checks the “Least Recently Seen” node in that full bucket. It pings it.

  • If the old node responds: It stays. The new node stays in the waiting list.
  • If the old node is dead: It is evicted. The new node is promoted from replacements to nodes.

This guarantees that our routing table is filled with robust, long-lived peers.

Finding Neighbors

Finally, the most used function in our entire DHT is findClosest. When we want to look up a key, we need to ask the nodes mathematically closest to it.
This function aggregates nodes from the target bucket, and then moves outwards to the adjacent buckets until sufficient candidates are found.

// src/peer/routing-table.js

findClosest(targetId, count = this.k) {
  const results = [];
  const start = this._bucketIndex(targetId);

  // We check buckets [start], [start+1], [start-1], [start+2]...
  // expanding outward from the target distance.
  for (let d = 0; d < this.buckets.length && results.length < count; d++) {
    const i = d % 2 === 0 ? start + d : start - d;
    if (i < 0 || i >= this.buckets.length) continue;

    const bucket = this.buckets[i];
    results.push(...bucket.nodes);
  }

  // Finally, sort everything by XOR distance to the target
  results.sort((a, b) =>
    compareDistance(xorDistance(a, targetId), xorDistance(b, targetId))
  );

  return results.slice(0, count);
}

The Core Logic (PeerNode)

We have the phone lines (WebRTC/ConnectionManager) and the phone book (RoutingTable). Now we need the operator.
PeerNode(src/peer/peer-node.js) is the brain of the operation. It is where the actual “Kademlia” happens, it orchestrates the complex operation of asking peers for information, collecting responses, and deciding where to go next. It is responsible for Iterative Lookups, Data Persistence, and Network Maintenance.

The Search: iterativeFindNode

This is the most critical algorithm in any DHT, when we want to find a node (or a piece of data/value), you can’t just ask any one of the neighbors and hope they know. We have to crawl the network, getting closer to the target one step at a time.

Kademlia uses an alpha-parallel search (where alpha=3 in this project).

The process is as follows:

  1. Shortlist: Pick the 20 closest nodes we already know.
  2. Parallel Query: Pick the top 3 (alpha) nodes we haven’t asked yet.
  3. Ask: Send FIND_NODE requests to them simultaneously.
  4. Update: They reply with their closest neighbors. We add these new nodes to our shortlist.
  5. Repeat: Sort the list, pick the next 3, and loop until we stop finding closer nodes.

This logic guarantees that even in a network of millions, we can find a target in O(log N) hops (usually just 3 or 4 jumps).

// src/peer/peer-node.js (Simplified)

async iterativeFindNode(targetNodeId) {
  let shortlist = this.routingTable.findClosest(targetNodeId, this.K);
  
  // The loop runs until we stop making progress or hit a max limit
  while (rounds++ < MAX_ROUNDS) {
    
    // Pick 'alpha' (3) unqueried nodes
    const batch = shortlist.filter(n => !queried.has(n)).slice(0, this.ALPHA);
    
    // Blast out requests in parallel
    const responses = await Promise.all(
      batch.map(node => this.sendFindNode(node, targetNodeId))
    );

    // Add new nodes discovered from responses to the shortlist
    for (const nodes of responses) {
      updateShortlist(shortlist, nodes);
    }

    // Sort by distance again
    shortlist.sort(/* sort by distance to target */);
  }

  return shortlist;
}

The Memory: storeValue and Quorums

A DHT isn’t useful if it loses data when a node goes offline. To prevent this, we never store data on just a single node. We store it on the k closest nodes (where k=20).

However, we don’t need all 20 nodes to confirm success. We wait for a Write Quorum (w).

  • k = 20
  • W = [k/2] = 10

This means if 10 nodes accept our data, we consider it saved. This ensures high availability. Even if 9 nodes crash immediately after the write, the data survives on the 10th node (and eventually with others).

// src/peer/peer-node.js

async storeValue(key, value) {
  // 1. Find the 20 closest nodes to the Key's hash
  const closest = await this.iterativeFindNode(keyId);
  
  const W = Math.ceil(this.K / 2); // 10
  let acks = 0;

  // 2. Send STORE command to them
  for (const hex of targets) {
    const ok = await this.conn.send(hex, /* STORE command */);
    
    if (ok) {
      acks++;
      // 3. Stop once we hit Quorum
      if (acks >= W) break;
    }
  }

  if (acks < W) {
    throw new Error(`STORE failed: quorum not reached (${acks}/${W})`);
  }
}

The Retrieval: findValue & Repair

Retrieving data (findValue) looks very similar to iterativeFindNode, with two key differences:

  1. Early Exit: If a peer replies with the Data instead of a list of nodes, the search stops immediately.
  2. Opportunistic Replication (Repair): This is a cool optimization.

Imagine you find the data on Node D. But Node A, Node B, and Node C were mathematically closer to the key but didn’t have it (maybe they were offline when it was published).
Since we are walking past A, B, and C anyway, we should fix that!

// src/peer/peer-node.js (Excerpt from findValue)

if (res.record) {
  // We found the data!
  bestRecord = res.record;

  // Look for a node that was CLOSER than the one who had the data
  const closer = shortlist.find(n => isCloser(n, responder));

  // "Store-back": Give the data to that closer node so the next person finds it faster
  if (closer) {
    this.conn.send(closer, encodeStore(keyId, bestRecord));
  }
}

This “Store-back” mechanism ensures that popular data naturally migrates to the nodes where it “belongs” (the closest ones), keeping the network efficient.

The Gardening: Maintenance Timers

This is my favorite example of emergent behavior derived from simple rules. A DHT is like a living organism. Nodes join, leave, and crash. Data expires. If we did nothing, the routing tables would rot and data would vanish.

In node.start(), several background timers are launched to act as janitors:

  1. Bucket Refresh: Pick a random ID in a bucket’s range and search for it. This forces us to find new peers in that specific area of the network, keeping the routing table full.
  2. Republish: If I am the original author of a piece of data, I must re-upload it every hour so peers know it’s still valid.
  3. Replica Repair: If I am holding data for someone else, I check if I am still one of the closest nodes. If not, I move the data to someone closer.
  4. Liveness Checks: Ping the oldest nodes in my routing table. If they don’t answer, evict them and replace them with fresh nodes.

Orchestration & Usage (Running the Swarm)

We have explored the code and understood the logic. Now, let’s play with it.

Developing a Distributed system is hard because we can’t easily run 50 copies of our app on our machine manually. We need Orchestration. The project includes a dedicated orchestration layer built using Docker Compose.

The Orchestrator

Instead of writing docker commands, the project includes a helper script(index.js) at the root directory.
When you run:

$ npm run docker -- up --peers 10

The script parses the arguments and executes:

$ docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d --scale peer=10

The magic word here is --scale. This tells Docker Compose to spin up 1 instance of the signalling server, 1 instance of the client, and 10 instances of the peer service.

Looking at docker-compose.yml, we see the network topology:

  • signalling: The bootstrap server. It exposes port 3000, so that, we can connect to it from our machine outside Docker.
  • client: The CLI tool. It depends on signalling. This can be run on our machine bare-metal.
  • peer: The worker nodes. They also depend on signalling.

Solving the “Thundering Herd” Problem

If we launch 50 peers simultaneously, they will all try to hit the WebSocket server and eventually each other at the same exact millisecond. This can cause network stall and connection timeouts.
To solve this, we add a small Jitter to our peer startup(peer-entry.sh). It spreads the load over 30 seconds, thus, ensuring the network bootstraps smoothly. This simulates how the network behaves in real life as all peers cannot start at the exact same time in real-life.

#!/bin/sh
# peer-entry.sh

# Generate a random delay between 0 and 30 seconds
DELAY=$(awk -v max="$STARTUP_DELAY_MAX" 'BEGIN{srand(); print int(rand()*(max+1))}')

echo "Startup delay: ${DELAY}s"
sleep "$DELAY"

# Start the node
exec "$@"

The Interactive Client

Once the swarm is running, we need a way to control it. We can check the logs manually, but that’s messy and hard. Instead, the project provides a “God Mode” client.
The client(src/peer/client.js) connects to the mesh just like any other peer and indeed behaves as a peer, but it exposes its routing table, events and commands in an interface directly to your terminal.

The CLI accepts several commands that trigger the internal PeerNode methods.

  • peers: Calls node.conn.getConnectedPeers(). Shows who we are directly connected to via WebRTC.
  • store <key> <value>: Triggers node.storeValue(). Will show “Store complete (quorum reached)” if it succeeds.
  • get <key>: Triggers node.findValue(). It will perform the lookup and print the result.
  • find <nodeId>: Triggers iterativeFindNode. Useful for debugging routing paths.
  • dump: Dumps the entire routing table (all buckets).

Putting it all together

Finally, here is how you simulate a Kademlia network on your machine.

Step 1: Start the Swarm
Boot up a network with 25 peers.

$ npm run docker -- all --peers 25

Wait about 30 seconds for the startup jitter to finish and the mesh to form.

Step 2: Enter the Client

# In a new terminal
$ npm run client

Step 3: Check Connections
Inside the client REPL:

> peers
Connected peers: [ 'a1b2...', 'c3d4...' ]

You should see at least one or two peers.

Step 4: Store Data
Let’s save a value into the cloud.

> store 67 "My value"
Store complete (quorum reached)

Behind the scenes, our client hashed “67”, found the 10 closest nodes among the 25 running containers, and replicated the data to them.

Step 5: Retrieve Data
Now, let’s ask the network for it back.

> get 67
Value found: "My value"

Step 6: Scale Up
Want to see how it handles growth? Leave the client open, and in another terminal run:

$ npm run docker -- up --peers 35

Docker will add 10 new peers to the existing network. The existing nodes will see them, add them to buckets, and the network topology will evolve automatically.

Real-world limitations

While WebRTC-DHT is a fully functional Kademlia implementation, it is designed for education and prototyping, not high-stakes production environments. If you plan to build the next IPFS or BitTorrent, you must address these constraints:

  1. NAT Traversal (STUN only): This project relies solely on public STUN servers (stun.l.google.com). This works for most home connections but will fail behind strict corporate firewalls or Symmetric NATs. A production system requires TURN servers to relay traffic when direct P2P connections fail.
  2. Memory-Only Storage: Data is stored in a JavaScript Map. If a node crashes or the container restarts, its specific shard of data is lost. Real systems must persist data to disk (e.g., LevelDB, SQLite) so that data survives application restarts.
  3. Security & Auth: There is no authentication mechanism, we trust all nodes. Anyone who knows the signalling server address can join the swarm. This makes the network vulnerable to Sybil Attacks (flooding the network with fake nodes to poison routing tables) or data tampering.
  4. Performance: Node.js with the wrtc binding is heavy. High-throughput distributed systems are typically implemented in Systems Languages (Rust, Go, C++) to avoid Garbage Collection pauses and minimize memory footprint per peer.

Conclusion

We have walked through the entire stack of WebRTC-DHT:

  1. Architecture: We saw how the code separates Networking, Routing, and Logic.
  2. Hybrid Signalling: We learned how to bootstrap via WebSockets and switch to P2P signalling.
  3. Routing Table: We explored XOR distance, buckets, and LRU eviction.
  4. Core Logic: We dissected the iterative lookup and quorum storage algorithms.
  5. Orchestration: We used Docker to simulate a swarm and handle thundering herds.

This project serves as a compact, readable reference for anyone wanting to understand how decentralized networks like IPFS or BitTorrent actually work under the hood.

Happy Hacking!

item.content:encoded:
As WordPress continues to evolve, so does the way we design and build websites. With the introduction of Full Site Editing (FSE), we’ve entered a new era where Block Themes and Block Patterns play a central role in how our sites look and function.

Let’s dive into what Block Themes and Block Patterns are, how they differ, and how we can use them to create more flexible and beautiful websites.

What Are WordPress Block Themes?

Block Themes are a new type of WordPress theme that are built entirely with blocks. These themes leverage the power of the Gutenberg block editor to allow us to customize every part of our site—from headers and footers to templates and content areas—without writing custom PHP templates.

Key Features of Block Themes:

  • Fully compatible with Full Site Editing (FSE)
  • Use of theme.json for global settings and styles
  • All templates and parts are created using blocks (.html files)
  • High design flexibility without needing a child theme

A Basic Structure of a Block Theme:

my-block-theme/
├── block-templates/
│   ├── index.html
│   └── single.html
├── block-template-parts/
│   ├── header.html
│   └── footer.html
├── patterns/
│   └── test.html
├── styles/
│   └── style.css
├── functions.php
├── style.css
├── theme.json

Example of theme.json in a Block Theme:


{
  "version": 2,
  "settings": {
    "color": {
      "palette": [
        {
          "slug": "primary",
          "color": "#0073aa",
          "name": "Primary"
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "styles": {
    "elements": {
      "h1": {
        "typography": {
          "fontSize": "2.5rem"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

This file gives us centralized control over global styles like fonts, colors, and spacing—without editing any CSS.

What Are WordPress Block Patterns?

Block Patterns are predefined collections of blocks that we can insert into pages or posts to speed up the design process. Think of them like reusable design sections—call to actions, hero sections, testimonials—that can be dropped in with one click.

Why We Love Block Patterns:

  • Reusable and modular
  • Speeds up page design
  • Customizable after insertion
  • Encourages consistent design

Registering a Custom Block Pattern in a Theme:

We can register patterns by adding a PHP file in the patterns/ directory and hooking into it in functions.php.

Example: patterns/call-to-action.php

<?php
register_block_pattern(
    'mytheme/call-to-action',
    array(
        'title'       => __('Call to Action', 'mytheme'),
        'description' => _x('A full-width call to action section.', 'Block pattern description', 'mytheme'),
        'content'     => '<!-- wp:group {"align":"full","backgroundColor":"primary","className":"cta"} -->
                            <div class="wp-block-group alignfull cta has-primary-background-color">
                              <h2>Ready to start your journey?</h2>
                              <p>Join us today and build your future.</p>
                              <a class="wp-block-button__link" href="/signup">Get Started</a>
                            </div>
                          <!-- /wp:group -->',
        'categories'  => array('call-to-action'),
    )
);

Block Themes vs Classic Themes

Best Practices When Using Block Themes and Patterns

  • Use theme.json to manage styles globally.
  • Keep templates modular—use template parts for headers, footers, etc.
  • Take advantage of WordPress’s native block patterns directory.
  • Encourage team members to reuse patterns for brand consistency.

Conclusion

Block Themes and Block Patterns aren’t just buzzwords—they’re the future of WordPress. Whether we’re building for clients or crafting our own sites, these tools give us greater flexibility, faster development, and more power over design—all while embracing a no-code/low-code philosophy.
